title: The Disappearing Christian Middle East, Part V: The Holy Land — When Christians Leave the Birthplace of Christianity - International Christian Concern
content:
Every December, Elias watches pilgrims pour into Bethlehem. From the doorway of his family’s small olivewood shop, he hears church bells ringing above the old stone buildings. He watches visitors walk toward the Church of the Nativity. Some have traveled thousands of miles for the chance to stand in the city where Christians believe Jesus was born. For Elias, however, Bethlehem is not a pilgrimage destination. It is home. His grandfather carved crosses and nativity scenes from olivewood, and his father expanded the business and began selling religious gifts to tour groups. Elias grew up sweeping sawdust from the shop floor, learning English phrases from tourists, and attending church with his family on Sundays. His grandparents are buried nearby; his children were baptized there. Nearly every street carries a memory. Lately, however, Elias and his wife, Rania, have begun discussing something neither imagined when they married: leaving. Their oldest daughter has been accepted to a university overseas, their son talks about finding work in Europe, and tourism has collapsed again because of war and instability. Some months, the shop barely covers its expenses. Rania’s sister in Canada calls regularly, reminding them that jobs and opportunities exist there for the children. Elias usually changes the subject. Then one night, after the children had gone to bed, he and Rania sat at the kitchen table. She asked him a question he couldn’t easily answer: “What happens if the children leave? Do we stay here alone because our grandparents stayed?” From their window, they can see the outline of a church in the distance. The building will probably still be there decades from now. What Elias no longer knows is whether his family will be. For Christian families like this one, that question lies at the center of one of the most troubling transformations taking place in Christianity’s birthplace. At Christmas, the Christian world turns its eyes toward Bethlehem. Pilgrims walk through Manger Square, church bells ring above the narrow streets, and worshippers enter the Church of the Nativity, traditionally revered as the place where Jesus was born. Television cameras carry those images into Christian homes around the world, and for a few days it can appear that Christianity is flourishing in the city where its story began. But step away from the pilgrimage sites and another story emerges. The churches remain, but the people are becoming fewer. International Christian Concern (ICC) reported in 2025 that Christians once represented roughly 85% of Bethlehem’s population. Today, they make up only a small fraction of the city’s residents. The contradiction is difficult to ignore. Millions of Christians worldwide dream of visiting Bethlehem. Few places on earth are more closely associated with Christianity than the Holy Land. Bethlehem, Jerusalem, Nazareth, the Sea of Galilee, and the Mount of Olives are names spoken in churches worldwide every week. Yet, Christians living in these places now make up only a small percentage of the region’s population. Palestinian Christian communities trace their roots in the land through centuries of Christian history and include Greek Orthodox, Roman Catholic, Armenian, Syriac, Lutheran, Anglican, evangelical, and other traditions. Their presence extends far beyond churches. Christians have established schools, hospitals, universities, businesses, charities, and cultural institutions throughout the region. Generations of Christian families have worked as teachers, physicians, shopkeepers, craftsmen, clergy, business owners, and community leaders. Yet their numbers have steadily declined. In its examination of Bethlehem’s shrinking Christian community, ICC reported that Christians represented about 84% of Bethlehem’s population in 1947. By 2016, that figure had fallen to around 12%, while Christians represented less than 2% of the West Bank population. For Christians living in the Holy Land, a Christian family may live relatively close to one of the faith’s holiest sites and still struggle to reach it. Travel between Gaza, the West Bank, Jerusalem, and Israel is heavily regulated. Permits, checkpoints, security restrictions, and closures can affect whether Palestinian Christians can attend religious celebrations, visit relatives, work, or travel to churches. In 2019, ICC reported that Christians in Gaza faced uncertainty over whether permits would be issued allowing them to travel to Bethlehem for Christmas. Israeli authorities initially said they would not grant permits. They later approved some applications, citing security considerations. The irony is difficult to miss: A Christian living thousands of miles away finds it easier to visit Bethlehem than a Christian living relatively nearby. Movement restrictions are not the only reason Christians leave, but they become part of a larger accumulation of pressure. Political conflict, economic hardship, insecurity, religious tensions, and restrictions on everyday life can eventually turn the question from “How do we stay?” into something very different: “Why stay?” For Gaza’s already tiny Christian population, that question became far more urgent after Oct. 7, 2023. Hamas’s attack on Israel triggered a devastating war in Gaza, affecting the territory’s entire civilian population, and Christians were no exception. Before the war, Gaza was home to only around 1,000 Christians, most belonging to the Greek Orthodox community with a smaller Catholic population. As fighting intensified, churches became places of refuge. Families crowded into church compounds, which might offer some protection from the violence outside. Among those shelters was Saint Porphyrius Greek Orthodox Church, which has served Gaza’s Christian community for centuries. That month, an explosion struck a building within the church compound where civilians were sheltering, killing people inside. ICC later documented the suffering of Gaza’s Christian community, describing Christians seeking refuge at Saint Porphyrius and Holy Family Catholic Church as the war unfolded around them. These Christians faced the same bombardment, shortages, displacement, fear, and uncertainty affecting Gaza’s broader civilian population. But a community this small faces an additional problem: Every person matters demographically. A city containing millions of people may eventually recover substantial population losses after war. A religious community numbering only about 1,000 may not. The stories examined throughout this series are different, but the pattern is becoming familiar. The Islamic State group (ISIS) drove Christians from Iraq’s Nineveh Plains. War scattered Syria’s Christian communities. Economic collapse and political instability have pushed Lebanese Christians abroad. In Bethlehem, Jerusalem, the West Bank, and Gaza, conflict, insecurity, restrictions, economic hardship, and emigration continue to shrink ancient Christian populations. Different causes are producing a remarkably similar result: fewer Christians. Part six will move to places where this process has already advanced much further. These are lands where Christianity was once not merely present, but dominant — places where today only small Christian remnants remain. Their history offers perhaps the strongest warning of this entire series: A civilization does not always disappear because every monument is destroyed. Sometimes the churches survive, the crosses remain, and the history remains, but the Christians are gone. To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom. For interviews, please email us. title: England player ratings: How Three Lions played rated v Czech Republic - BBC
content: Harry Kane scored twice on his 125th appearance for England - but who else impressed? Harry Kane scored twice as England cruised to a comfortable 3-0 win over the Czech Republic in the Nations League at Wembley on Tuesday. Here's how I rated the players - and you can see how you scored them below. Jordan Pickford: Will return to Everton knowing his place is now under threat from James Trafford. Some shaky moments. 6 Trent Alexander-Arnold: Given another opportunity to impress and took it. Ability on the ball perfect for deep-lying opponents like the Czech Republic. 7 Jarell Quansah: Deployed in his favoured centre-back role and looked comfortable. Slowly becoming a fixture in the squad. 6 Marc Guehi: But for a couple of lapses, cruised through the game. title: International friendly match today: How to watch USA v Canada, TV channels & live stream Wednesday 6 October - The Guardian
content: How will the USA and Canada fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options Basking in the glow of a 3-0 win over Mexico on Saturday, the US men’s national team are in a good place right now. A fourth straight win would make this window a resounding success for Mauricio Pochettino and his players. Canada, however, have won their last two encounters with the USMNT, and are fresh from back-to-back victories over Chile and Peru. Jesse Marsch’s side have good reason to believe they can leave Minnesota with a third successive win. While this rivalry lacks the ferocity of the one between Mexico and the USA, Canada have more than proven themselves as a member of Concacaf’s elite in recent times with Marsch always keen to make a point to US Soccer after being passed over for the national team job. Here is your complete guide on how to watch Tuesday’s international friendly fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options. Pochettino’s youthful revolution has re-energised the USMNT after the 2026 World Cup with prospects such as Cavan Sullivan, Julian Hall and Diego Kochen all showing why they deserve to play an important role in the national team’s next cycle. After three games in little over a week, Pochettino is expected to rotate his team. This makes it difficult to predict the lineup that will take to the field on Tuesday. Nonetheless, the USMNT won’t be short of players hoping to make a good impression. Marsch says Canada “can beat just about anybody.” However, the visitors must ensure the transition moments fall in their favor otherwise the US could blow away another opponent, after scoring 11 times in their last three outings. Player to watch: Cavan Sullivan, USA - The 17-year-old was the star man (boy?) for the USMNT against Mexico, scoring his first international goal just a few days after making his first international start. Sullivan has shown he is ready to become a key figure for his country.

title: Liberal justices look for 'escape hatch' as high-stakes climate case lands at Supreme Court, experts say - Fox News
content:

Utah and Alabama attorneys general warn Colorado’s climate case could drive up costs nationwide, while former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee argues Americans harmed by climate change deserve their day in court. Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor's repeated questions concerning whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear a high-profile climate case that could expose oil companies to lawsuits across the country steered conservative lawyers to believe that the liberal justices are seeking an "off-ramp." "The fact that they kept going back to trying to create a jurisdictional problem tells me they don't feel confident that they have the votes in this space," Carrie Severino, president of JCN, a conservative judicial group, told Fox News Digital. "Jackson and Sotomayor were looking for an escape hatch." The Supreme Court began its new term Monday, hearing its first oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder, in which they will rule on whether state tort laws can be used to seek damages from oil companies for climate change, even when the alleged harms are occurring outside the state or continent. The justices will also rule on whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear this case now, as the case is still before the Colorado Supreme Court. The case before the high court is in an unusual procedural posture, meaning the justices could resolve it without ever reaching the blockbuster state-versus-federal power fight at its center. That dispute centers on whether Colorado can use its own laws to seek damages for alleged harms caused by emissions from other states or whether it's an issue for the federal government and Congress to regulate. Climate activist protesters gather outside the Supreme Court before oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder on Oct. 5, 2025. (Elaine Mallon/Fox News Digital) SUPREME COURT BEGINS NEW TERM WITH HIGH-PROFILE LOOK AT CLEAN AIR AND FEDERAL AUTHORITY "The questions by Jackson and Sotomayor trying to say it would be premature for the court to issue an opinion are simply the liberal justices trying to find an off-ramp for the case because they are afraid they will be outvoted on the main issue: does federal law such as the Clean Air Act preempt all state claims like those asserted here," Hans von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow with Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital. While questioning Suncor attorney Kannon Shanmugam, Jackson suggested the dispute may have reached the Supreme Court too soon, calling it "premature from the standpoint of this court exercising its jurisdiction." She also repeatedly questioned why the court couldn't wait to hear the case, saying the court doesn't "have the whole set of facts" and that the court doesn't "really know enough to be confident" that the theories posed are applicable. "It feels to me like the defendants ... are bringing it back to federal court before the state courts have really had a chance to sort out who is the source, what is their allegation with respect to how this causation is happening," Jackson told Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who argued in support of Suncor. Meanwhile, Sotomayor refused to drop her line of questioning on jurisdiction with Shanmugam, proposing that the Supreme Court send the case back to the Colorado Supreme Court. "If we're unsure of your characterization, because there's certainly a number of amici brief who disagree with that characterization, shouldn't we be certifying this question to the Colorado court instead of us deciding it? We have to be sure of our jurisdiction before we take it," Sotomayor said. Republican Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall told Fox News Digital it was clear that the liberal justices were trying to cast doubt on whether they have jurisdiction. Climate activists gather outside the Supreme Court for oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder on Oct. 5, 2026. (Elaine Mallon/Fox News Digital) SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA "Well, I think you saw both Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor try to find an out for this court, basically saying the court doesn't have jurisdiction at this stage of the case to be able to make a final ruling. I think that you saw the advocates on behalf of Suncor be able to distinguish that." If the Supreme Court declines to reach the federalism issue, the Colorado Supreme Court's ruling allowing Boulder's state-law claims to proceed would remain in place, leaving the broader question of how far states can use tort law to pursue climate claims against energy companies unresolved. Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Boulder attorney Kevin Russell on whether a Boulder win could trigger similar lawsuits nationwide. Russell said there are legal limits, but acknowledged to Justice Clarence Thomas that Boulder's theory could allow other fossil-fuel businesses to be sued. "The chief justice and the court do not like issuing rulings with no limiting principles, rulings that could open up unlimited litigation and claims. Kannon Shanmugam, the lawyer for Suncor, emphasized this again at the very end of the oral argument when he pointed out that there are not only 90,000 political jurisdictions that could sue, but individuals could also sue claiming damages from global warming," von Spakovsky said. "And he also pointed out something the conservative majority frowns upon: that Boulder is trying to resolve a major policy issue in the courts instead of in the legislative branches," von Spakovsky continued. Conservative lawyers believe that Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor are seeking an "off-ramp." (Getty Images) SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE Supporters of Suncor say the lawsuits could "bankrupt" oil companies and cause the price for consumers to go up. "It's to basically create a carbon tax on both producers and emitters across the country, which would include, by the way, my cattlemen in Alabama producing beef for our country, those that are creating concrete to be able to build structures and be able to grow our economy," Marshall told Fox News. "They ultimately want to bankrupt that industry to have their preferred climate change policies be in play." "They're literally addressing behavior that takes place all over the world," Utah Attorney General Derek Brown told Fox News Digital. "They want to regulate not just what happens in Colorado, but what happens in my state of Utah or in Saudi Arabia. That's not the way the system works. So, really, this case comes down to one main issue and that is who gets to decide things like energy policy. And ultimately, under our system, it should be Congress." Meanwhile, Boulder alleged ExxonMobil and Suncor knew for decades about the climate risks associated with fossil fuels but misled the public about those risks. The communities estimate that taxpayers could face more than $100 million in costs to adapt to climate-related impacts, including wildfires, drought and damage to roads and other infrastructure. Former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a Democrat and longtime advocate for aggressive action on climate change, argued those costs are already being felt by communities across the country. "As governor, I've worked with so many families who've lost their homes," Inslee told Fox News Digital. "So many communities have essentially burned down, and they ought to be able to have a day in court to hear the evidence, to determine whether the lies of the oil and gas industry legitimately, they make it so that they're held accountable." The complaint pointed to a 1977 internal memo from ExxonMobil that circulated among the company's highest-level managers. The memo reported that "current scientific opinion overwhelmingly favors" that fossil fuels contribute to the rise in CO2 emissions. "Their own scientists knew that their product was dangerous, that it was going to cause more fires. And they knew this for decades, 1967, their own scientists told them it could be catastrophic, so they knew about it, they lied about it," Inslee said. "Now it's an American right to be in court. Nobody should bar an American from their day in court." Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics. title: Pushback: Ryan Whitney v. Maura Healey: Don’t ban natural kratom leaves - Greenfield Recorder
content: Sign up for the Recorder's FREE morning newsletter and get essential news each day. On Aug. 13, 2026, Massachusetts Department of Public Health Commissioner Robbie Goldstein, at the direction of Gov. Maura Healey, issued an emergency regulation under the state’s Controlled Substance Act — on a temporary one-year basis — placing kratom tree leaves on a Schedule 1 banned substance list as an imminent hazard to the public safety. Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) is a tree native to Southeast Asia within the coffee family (Rubiaceae), which has been used for centuries. In its natural leaf form, it contains trace amounts of 7-hydroxymitagynine (7-OH) and derivatives of mitragynine. Kratom is used by as many as 24 million Americans for its stimulant-type effects, such as increased alertness, pain relief and sedation. It is also used for conditions such as anxiety and depression. Many “synthesized” products labeled as kratom have been adulterated and mass-marketed as “gummy” candies with popular artificial fruit flavorings, and much higher concentrations of 7-OH and mitragynine. “Consumers have no reliable way of knowing what compounds a specific product contains, or how potent it may be,” DPH warns. On Aug. 18, Healey issued a press release noting that “dangerous kratom products” were now under an order restricting the sale of kratom across the state. Local boards of health, including Greenfield, were given “additional authority to take enforcement action against retailers selling kratom products… They are illegal to possess, distribute or manufacture.” “Regular kratom use,” Healey said, “can also lead to physical dependence and withdrawal symptoms similar to opioid withdrawal.” At the federal level, the Drug Enforcement Administration has not classified natural kratom leaf with trace 7-OH as a Schedule 1 substance. DEA’s order regulating synthetic kratom products went into effect on Aug. 26. On July 29, the Commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration, Dr. Marty Makary wrote a column in the NY Post: “To be clear, the kratom plant leaf, which contains trace amounts of 7-OH and has been consumed for centuries, is not our focus at the FDA. Rather, we are seeking to remove a dangerous synthetic opioid from retail shelves nationwide.” On Aug. 24, Greenfield activist Ryan Whitney filed a complaint in Franklin County Superior Court against the governor and the DPH Commissioner for issuing a kratom order “arbitrary, capricious, and in excess of statutory authority.” Whitney stated he has “used natural, unadulterated botanical kratom responsibly for approximately 8 years to manage chronic physical pain, treat severe anxiety and depression, support physical health stability, and maintain daily living.” Whitney asserts he “does not utilize kratom for intoxication or recreational purposes.” Before trying natural leaf kratom, he “tried numerous conventional pharmaceutical medications for anxiety, depression, and pain management, none of which provided therapeutic relief or stability.” On the web or with our app, the Greenfield Recorder provides award-winning, essential local coverage from arts and sports to breaking news and opinion. You get unlimited access to it all, including archives and our popular e-Edition. Whitney charges that the defendants acted “without a rational scientific foundation” by banning unadulterated botanical leaf “based on toxicological data primarily driven by synthetic derivatives.” The governor’s order resulted in “immediate criminalization of personal possession,” which forced Whitney to face criminal penalties “for maintaining a long-standing personal healthcare tool in his own home.” Last February, Mac Haddow, a Senior Fellow on Public Policy at the American Kratom Association (AKA), testified before Congress: “The question before you is not whether dangerous synthetic opioids should be controlled. They should. The question is whether in doing so, we accidentally ban a natural botanical product used responsibly by millions of Americans — and in the process recreate the very harms of prohibition that history has repeatedly warned us against.” Twenty-two states have enacted forms of the Kratom Consumer Protection Act. Rhode Island banned kratom in 2015, but repealed its law last year. They now have a Kratom Consumer Protection Act. The AKA model recommends that chemically synthesized 7-OH should be banned; products exceeding 2% of total alkaloid content should be banned; kratom leaf products containing trace 7-OH should be available only to people over 21. On Sept. 21, the Boston City Council deliberated on a proposed ordinance to ban synthetic kratom products, but keep natural leaf off the Schedule 1 ban list, available to people over age 21. One of the last people to testify was Ryan Whitney. He told city councilors that banning natural leaf kratom has “put me in so much fear. I’ve been having panic attacks. I can’t drive in the car because I’m scared if I travel too far, and I have it in my car and I get pulled over, they’ll want to search the vehicle.” Ryan now faces a prison sentence for just having natural kratom tree leaves in his glove compartment. title: Sheila V. Treeby - Montgomery Stryker
content: Sheila Sales Treeby, 6-10-1966, passed away at her home in West Laramie, Wyoming, on August 31, 2026, at sixty years of age. A native of Saint Louis, Missouri’s Leduc Street, Sheila was a 1984 graduate of Kennard Navy ROTC Academy High School while working part-time at Children’s Hospital, Boatman Bank and as a summer intern at KMOX-KHTR-KLOU Radio Station where she became fond of making runs for their sports director, Jack Buck, a future hall-of-famer.  A long-delayed nursing career was finally realized in 2012-2013 with an Associate Degree of Science, Sheridan College, membership in Phi Theta Kappa Academic Honor Society, a state CNA license and supervisor’s consent to LPN level wages. Sheila moved to Laramie in 2018 to pursue a double major in Nursing and Social Work from the University, but was slowed by congestive heart failure during the pandemic. Sheila is survived by her husband, Cameron E. Treeby; her mother, Cleola Sales, Buffalo, Wyoming; brother and sister, Willie Phillips and Veronica Phillips, both of St. Louis; sons Alexander Parks, Laramie, and Donovan Smith of Palmdale, California. A Committal Service will be held Friday, October 30, 2:00 P.M. at West Texas Veterans’ Cemetery in Lubbock, Texas. Memorial donations to: Outriders Ranch Dog Association, P.O. Box 2336, Laramie, Wyoming, 82073, in Sheila’s memory.  Visit Outridersranch.org website for more information. Copyright Ⓒ Montgomery Stryker Funeral Home

title: OPT Deploys Greensea IQ Bayonet 150 AUGV Offshore From Modified WAM-V 16 USV - Ocean News & Technology
content: Ocean Power Technologies, Inc., a leader of maritime operational infrastructure and autonomous ocean systems, has announced the successful completion of a proof of concept requested by Greensea IQ involving the offshore deployment of the amphibious Bayonet 150 Autonomous Underwater Ground Vehicle (AUGV) from a modified WAM-V® 16 unmanned surface vessel (USV). OPT modified the WAM-V 16 to transport and deploy the 300-pound Bayonet 150. During the test, the WAM-V carried the vehicle offshore, initiated a remotely triggered release, and safely deployed its umbilical. After deployment, Bayonet operated under Greensea IQ’s control system and completed its transit from the offshore release point to the beach. The proof of concept focused on transport, deployment, and safe separation between vehicles. Bayonet is designed for amphibious and surf-zone operations relevant to mine countermeasures and other littoral missions. “Greensea IQ brought us a specific deployment challenge: transport a 300-pound amphibious vehicle offshore and release it safely for independent transit to the beach,” said Jason Weed, Chief Operating Officer of OPT. “We modified the WAM-V 16 to support the vehicle, its remotely triggered deployment, and its umbilical. Completing that sequence demonstrates the value of WAM-V as adaptable mobile infrastructure for specialized partner systems.” “Paired with a Bayonet 150 AUGV, the WAM-V USV can now take on seabed missions with greater flexibility. The Bayonet Autonomous Ground Vehicle (AUGV) deploys straight from the USV’s open chassis, creating one unmanned system that can cover the surface and work the seabed in the same mission,” said Paco Santana, VP of Business Development for Greensea IQ. Tracy Pagliara, Acting President and CEO of OPT, added: “We believe the test demonstrates WAM-V 16’s role as a modular surface transport and deployment platform. title: Oral Argument Recap: Suncor v. Boulder - Transnational Litigation Blog
content: Photo by mana5280(opens in new tab) on Unsplash(opens in new tab) On Monday, the Supreme Court opened its new Term with oral arguments in Suncor v. County Commissioners of Boulder County(opens in new tab) (for background on the case, check out our preview post). Justice Alito did not participate as he has recused himself. Here are some takeaways as we await the Court’s decision. Kannon Shanmugam, arguing for the petitioner/defendant gas and oil companies, opened with and kept returning to “the Constitution’s prohibition on extraterritorial regulation,” which he at one point termed “venerable.” He defined this extraterritoriality principle as prohibiting litigation of conduct that is not directed at the state, causes diffuse harm, and has only a “severely attenuated” causal nexus to the state. None of the Justices seemed receptive to this theory. As Kevin Russell, arguing on behalf of the respondent/plaintiff localities, repeatedly and correctly emphasized, such concerns are already addressed through choice of law, the dormant Commerce Clause, personal jurisdiction, and tort law. I counted at least five Justices who were likewise frustrated by the blurring of these doctrines and the lack of constitutional or precedential hook for a broader “extraterritoriality principle.” As Justice Kagan memorably put it, “So there’s a default rule [against state extraterritoriality] that was part of the plan of the Convention. And I suppose it’s like:  Wow, like, where is the text for that? Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that?  Where’s the anything for that?” When Chief Justice Roberts, Justice Kagan, and Justice Gorsuch all pressed Shanmugam on the distinction between this proposed extraterritoriality principle and choice of law, he kept falling back on preemption arguments specific to environmental law—a slippage that Kagan explicitly called out in another one of my favorite exchanges: JUSTICE KAGAN: … And as you’re pressed on the extraterritorial aspect, you go back to your environmental theory. So is it really that your extraterritorial theory cannot stand alone? SHANMUGAM: Like my children, I love both of our theories equally, Justice Kagan. JUSTICE KAGAN: Well, but if … that’s true, then you can’t answer questions about the extraterritorial theory by referring to the nature of air and water regulation. Luckily for petitioners, its preemption theory might have more legs. Kavanaugh made clear that he reads the Court’s precedents as establishing that “interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law unless Congress specifically preserves state law.” But even then, he kept noting, the Court has permitted such state common law pollution claims to proceed under the law of the emitting state. If that’s correct, then the problem with this lawsuit is not the invocation of state law, but the invocation of the wrong state’s law.  While Justice Kavanaugh developed this line of reasoning repeatedly and emphatically, it requires flipping the standard presumption against preemption into a presumption of preemption. Further, as Justice Jackson pointed out, it is not yet settled which state’s law would apply in this case: respondents didn’t plead any particular state’s law, and the trial court has yet to make its choice-of-law determination. Justice Barrett likewise seemed interested in a preemption analysis, though perhaps a little less ready that Kavanaugh to flip the default rule. Gorsuch wondered aloud whether the Solicitor General wasn’t leading with preemption because there was something wrong with that line of argument. There are indeed a lot of questions that would have to be addressed for the petitioners to win on preemption, even beyond those raised by Kavanaugh’s approach. The EPA has repealed its endangerment finding, reasoning that the Clean Air Act does not address greenhouse gas emissions and climate change—a development that came up repeatedly during the arguments. Both Gorsuch and Barrett seemed to accept that this would leave space for residual common law claims, though they both seemed to think that law would be federal common law, not state law. Even if that’s true, what would be the content of that federal common law? The respondents, for their part, argued that the Clean Air Act—and any statutory preemption that follows in its wake—is simply inapplicable because they framed their allegations in terms of deceptive marketing, not emissions. (Sotomayor seemed to agree on this point, while Roberts was skeptical of the distinction.) The petitioners were unwilling to accept Kavanaugh’s preemption approach, however, because they want the Court to rule that state law can never be invoked in cases related to climate change. Why? Shanmugam was explicit: because “there are dozens of these cases out there.” Holding that this case is preempted might only give plaintiffs a roadmap for how to properly plead their climate change claims in other cases. Some of the Justices were explicitly sympathetic to this practical concern. Kavanaugh called the respondents “cavalier” about the burdens of litigation, expressing concern that these climate change cases might bankrupt the defendants. As Roberts pressed Russell, “presumably, if you prevail, the next day, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit, they’ll probably copy your pleadings …. how do you think that will work out on the ground?” In response, Russell noted the plaintiffs would still have to satisfy the dormant Commerce Clause, choice of law rules, personal jurisdiction, and proximate causation, and he pointed to the experience of asbestos and other product liability suits. “I don’t think there’s anything in the Constitution,” he summed up, “that says preemption arises from — whenever, you know, a state law, if copied in other states, could cause a lot of litigation.” I am a bit worried that Roberts, Kavanaugh, and Thomas (and possibly others) were so concerned about the door the Court could leave open for climate change litigation. Roberts did not explain why he thinks “asbestos is a little different”: those cases also overwhelmed the federal courts, posed difficult attribution problems, and did bankrupt large companies. But there was no broad constitutional prohibition on the applicability of state law to those claims. There are real dangers that a broad holding in favor of the petitioners in this case could have sweeping effects on the scope of state power. Before the Court can reach either the question of preemption or the existence of an “extraterritoriality principle,” however, it will first have to decide that it has the authority to hear this case. That requires finding that the Colorado Supreme Court’s decision reviewing the state trial court’s decision not to dismiss due to preemption is a final judgment under 28 U.S.C. § 1957(opens in new tab). Further, if the state court decision is treated as a final judgment independent from the underlying lawsuit, does that decision by itself harm the defendants so as to provide them with standing under Article III? Justice Thomas’s initial question for both the petitioners and the Solicitor General was whether the Court has jurisdiction to hear this claim. Jackson repeatedly returned to the prematurity of this appeal and the problems caused by the procedural posture (including, for example, the lack of a choice-of-law determination). On standing, the petitioners argue they should not have to bear the heavy costs of litigation while awaiting review of their preemption arguments and other federal defenses following a final judgment on the merits. That litigation by itself is a constitutionally cognizable injury seems like a dangerously broad principle to adopt. In sum, Kavanaugh, Barrett, and Gorsuch seem to be interested in a preemption-based rationale for shutting down this lawsuit, though it is unclear whether they will agree amongst themselves on precisely how to reach that result. Though Roberts asked little about preemption, his pragmatic concerns coupled with his obvious distaste for the petitioners’ proposed “extraterritoriality principle” might lead him to support a creative preemption holding.  Meanwhile, Kagan, Sotomayor, and Jackson seemed utterly unconvinced by all of the petitioners’ arguments, from jurisdiction to preemption to new constitutional principles. That leaves Justice Thomas as the likely deciding vote (as a tie would leave the Colorado Supreme Court’s judgment undisturbed). While Thomas pressed the petitioners on jurisdiction, he also pressed the respondents on the limits of their approach to state tort law. He may be less willing than Roberts to join a creative preemption rationale, however, given the opinion he authored last Term in Hencely v. Fluor Corp.(opens in new tab) (2026), which rejected a new doctrine of “battlefield preemption.” (Notably, Roberts and Kavanaugh joined Alito’s dissent in that case—a dissent motivated primarily by pragmatic concerns.) It may be that Suncor produces a set of fractured decisions, not unlike the Court’s most recent dormant Commerce Clause decision in National Pork Producers Council v. Ross (2023). But one thing seems fairly clear: the petitioners are not going to get the sweeping victory they would like. If oil and gas companies want to shut down climate change litigation, their best bet is Congress. title: V/H/S/Mixtape review – murderous puppets pull the strings in mixed bag of gory music-themed mini-movies - The Guardian
content: Metal band Gwar host this instalment of the horror series, which serves up darkly humorous movie morsels that would struggle to frighten a toddler The latest in the long-running horror-feature series is, as per usual, a decidedly diverse ragbag of shorts, strung together with the thinnest of connective tissue. The theme this go-round seems to be music and sound, so it sort of makes sense that hosting duties for the interstitial bits fall to the goofy metal band Gwar, its assorted members met here cracking Halloween dad jokes in their trademark extravagant outfits. The five mini movies vary significantly in length as well as quality. Flying Lotus’s stop-motion exercise Another Cabin posits a young boy in a rural cabin living with a mean old grannie who tries to push him forward when a tentacled demon tears the roof of the house in search of a snack. The characters’ resemblance to the cast of early 2000s series The PJs is slightly jarring, given this is such a different register, but the brevity works in its favour. In contrast Renee Zhan’s Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance, the opener, drags on a bit, but has a reasonable gags-to-gore ratio in its tale of murderous puppets taking revenge on visiting studio execs who would dare to “reimagine” some ageing IP best left dormant. The funniest gag is the bright major-scale title song the puppets (designed by Jim Henson’s Creature Shop) sing about how all things must die. Venerable cinematographer turned director Ernest Dickerson (who filmed several key Spike Lee films including Do the Right Thing and Malcolm X) turns the unsurprisingly beautifully shot and designed but thinly written amuse-bouche The Music of Mr Sze. This features Jihad Brent as an aspiring film-maker who becomes bewitched by the violin melodies emanating from the bedsit of his upstairs neighbour (Alex Hsu), a story that escalates into a fantasia of trippy but borderline incomprehensible imagery. Far more straightforward narratively but repetitive, Death Tone (directed by RZA) stars Neela Jolene as the daughter of a famed music producer who follows her late father’s instructions – and dips into his narcotic supply – to make the perfect song, featuring the screams of agony from a range of random victims. RZA is clearly having a jolly chuckle to himself over gags that might crack them up in the sound booth, but they don’t travel as well as he seems to think. Somewhere in the middle of this package David Moreau’s Heartbeat is a snoozy riff on a theme from Edgar Allan Poe, about obnoxious YouTubers who get trapped in a Bulgarian military base. Throughout the practical effects are over the top, rubbery and absurd; so much so they would struggle to frighten a toddler, but with its unpleasantly warped humour it’s not really for kids anyway. V/H/S/Mixtape is on Shudder and AMC+ from 9 October The Guardian has something US newsrooms increasingly don’t: guaranteed independence. title: V/H/S/Mixtape Review: The Horror Anthology Series Finds Its Groove [Beyond Fest 2026] - SlashFilm
content: By this point, the "V/H/S" franchise has gained a reputation as a reliably entertaining horror anthology. As of the latest entry in the series, "V/H/S/Mixtape," the franchise boasts 9 films produced over the last 14 years. Essentially, "V/H/S" began as a way of combining a lo-fi, analog aesthetic with found footage. The films then became a great showcase for emerging indie horror filmmakers (folks that are now household genre names like Radio Silence and Adam Wingard got a big push from their "V/H/S" work), as well as veterans who sought to take advantage of the creative opportunities the series afforded. So while the franchise has always had a general sense of cohesion, the series was admittedly confused for many years about whether or not it had creative tissue connecting each entry, or if they were just free-for-all grab bags. The first three films in the series attempted to establish a very, very loose mythology surrounding the various short horror films that comprise a "V/H/S" entry, implying they were cursed videotapes of some kind. When producer Josh Goldbloom and Shudder revived the franchise in 2021 with "V/H/S/94," the echoes of that mythos were still there, albeit faint. After the series enjoyed success by theming the next two entries around a particular year, the central theme became more defined with 2024's sci-fi "V/H/S/Beyond." Now, after last year's "Halloween" and this year's music-centric "Mixtape," Goldbloom has helped the series finally find a thematic groove as reliable as the series' positive reputation. So, while "V/H/S/Mixtape" may not be the best entry in the series, it's the one that feels like it has the best theme so far. I'm of the opinion that there has yet to be a wholly bad "V/H/S" entry. That said, there's no doubt that even my favorite films in the series are uneven. What producer Josh Goldbloom and company have done with "Mixtape" is continue the winning streak they've been on with "Beyond" and "Halloween," giving the various filmmakers involved a theme that's broad enough to inspire variety but one that's more specific than just a random past year. The theme of "Mixtape" is music, and this results in segments which either involve a song, musical instruments, or explore other eerie aspects of sound. The wraparound segment, directed by Flying Lotus and starring the spooky heavy metal band GWAR, is the franchise's most successful wraparound film in the way it naturally integrates the various short segments via a fictional vintage MTV-style program. It's still pretty loose, sure, but it helps the movie flow naturally, and the band's Troma-style gross-out humor is a far better choice for a "V/H/S" wraparound than something trying to build scares in chunks over the course of the feature. This wraparound leads to the inclusion of some original music videos, and the hiring of folks already familiar with the form (Flying Lotus, RZA, and the band Ghost's Tobias Forge) results in some fabulous work. Forge's awesome music video with his band Repugnant, "Premature Burial," feels like a death metal riff on controversial German filmmaker Jörg Buttgereit's work, which is an unexpected treat. "V/H/S/Mixtape" is pretty much hitting the nail on the head with its titular theme, as sequencing an anthology movie is akin to making a mixtape. In both, the presentation is just as important as the art itself, for sometimes the right thing can come along at the wrong moment. That's unfortunately the case with "The Music of Mr. Sze," written and directed by legendary filmmaker Ernest Dickerson. Loosely based on a pair of H.P. Lovecraft short stories, "Mr. Sze" is a segment which takes its time building its premise and revealing its game. Sadly, the segment appears around the midpoint of the film, and feels a little deflating in its more deliberate pacing than if it had appeared at the beginning. Conversely, David Moreau's "Heartbeat" is a little too bold in its presentation compared to the film around it. Shot with a unique lens and camera setup that feels like a combination of a selfie stick and a GoPro, the segment takes a lot of getting used to visually and rhythmically. This means that by the time you've gotten onto its wavelength and understand what is going on, the short is practically over. Another segment, Flying Lotus' animated music video "Another Cabin," also feels adrift within the film. These segments are still worthwhile individually, and their bumpiness is more a byproduct of the movie's anthology format, the revolving door of directors, and so on. So if there's one aspect where the "V/H/S" films can still improve, it's in keeping an eye on the the whole as much as possible. Where "V/H/S/Mixtape" really shines is in its greatest segments, as they feel like the perfect result between overarching theme and the filmmakers' individual expression. Renee Zhan and Zoe Cooper's "Dance, Dance, Dance, Dance" includes work by Jim Henson's Creature Shop, marking one of the rare instances where the company's talents are utilized for a decidedly adult theme. As a result, this segment feels like the next word in kindertrauma horror after Casper Kelly's surprise hit, "Buddy." Meanwhile, RZA and Matt Landsman's "Death Tone" is a nasty, clever little tale that boasts some impressively bizarre kills and practical effects. As with his earlier film this year, "One Spoon of Chocolate," RZA continues to demonstrate his innate understanding of exploitation cinema tropes while creating something that feels more unique than beholden to retro homage. With "V/H/S/Mixtape," the series feels like it's finally found a comfortable groove for itself, blending its showcase of new and veteran filmmakers with a theme that's simultaneously unifying and malleable. This is why I have such trepidation about the 10th film in the series, which has been announced as some sort of collaboration with the previously unrelated fictional secret organization known as the SCP Foundation. Given that "Mixtape" can be seen as the third in a "trilogy," it feels like "V/H/S" might be revolving yet again with this next film, pivoting into new territory as it did before with "94" and then "Beyond." Hopefully, the recipe for success that's been found with "Mixtape" won't be forgotten on the next go round. "V/H/S/Mixtape" is streaming on Shudder beginning October 9, 2026.

title: We Got GTA V Running On Web Browser Before GTA 6 - Wccftech
content:
Who would have thought that running an intensive game like GTA V on a web browser would be possible? It felt amazing seeing GTA: Vice City running in a web browser last year, which allowed players to play the demo without downloading the actual game. However, witnessing a much more intensive and feature-packed GTA title in a web browser is far more shocking. If you have ever imagined playing GTA V in a web browser, then yes, it has been made possible. Someone just made a project that runs the title in a web browser without installing the game locally on the PC. It was live on PlayGTA5.com briefly, and several users confirmed running the game in their web browsers. The account @4k_isn demonstrated running the game in Google Chrome on an Apple machine with an M3 Pro chip. The browser version reportedly downloaded 700 MB before starting, although additional assets could be downloaded during the gameplay. That makes the achievement more interesting because users weren't downloading the full PC installation. One might think it could have been a conventional cloud gaming service, but the available evidence suggests that the game was being executed locally within the browser. Videocardz says WebAssembly might be involved in this, but it's still unclear whether the original executable was recompiled, translated through a compatibility layer, or modified specifically for browser-based execution. Many users have commented and posted screenshots of running GTA V in their browsers in the thread, but a lot of them couldn't access it since it was taken down soon after. The poster said Rockstar might have taken it down, but when you visit the website, you might see a message like "Who wants the source code?" The website doesn't load anymore, which might be due to high traffic, and it's unlikely that it will come back. title: Where to Watch: England v Czechia - Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha Included In Matchday Squad - Yahoo Sports
content: The Three Lions play their final game of this extended three-week international break as they take on Czechia for the second time at Wembley Stadium. Both sides will come into this game with polar opposite form and morale, with Czechia having not picked up any points so far in their first three fixtures, while England will be full of confidence after an emphatic win away in Rijeka. Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha was part of a record-breaking England side as they put seven goals, without reply, past a poor Croatia team, setting a new record for the biggest winning margin in UEFA Nations League history, and to do it away from home was all the more impressive. While there were only 6,000 Croatian schoolchildren and 100 England fans in the stadium, due to the home team's supporters having a one-match ban after abusive language was heard during a Nations League game against France in 2025, the victory for Thomas Tuchel's England side was seismic. However, Anfield starboy Rio Ngumoha did not feature for his country in this impressive win, not starting or coming off the bench for the Three Lions. So this may give LFC fans some hope that Ngumoha could be set to play a role in the final game against Czechia, where a win would all but secure England a top-two spot. The tricky left winger recently turned 18 years old, meaning he is now eligible to sign a professional, long-term deal with the Reds. It was previously reported by several journalists that talks between the club and Ngumoha's representatives were ongoing and that they were progressing well. David Ornstein also came out during September going into some detail about Rio Ngumoha's current situation at Liverpool, and he explained that the teenage sensation had shown no signs, up to that point, of unhappiness or a desire to depart Anfield in the near future. And despite his current contract running until 2028, the Merseyside club determined to hold on to him long into the future. When away on international duty, Ngumoha has spoken about the reason why he chose the move to Liverpool over the likes of Chelsea, Arsenal and Bayern Munich, who have all expressed interest in him, or in Chelsea's case, actually had him in their academy. "Liverpool was always the RIGHT option and really the ONLY option. I knew that if I went there, I'd get the opportunity and the pathway to showcase what I can do, and it looks like so far it's paid off." - Rio Ngumoha on choosing Liverpool over other options This match will take place on Tuesday 6th October 2026, and will kick off at 7:45 pm (BST), with it available to watch for free on ITV1 and ITVX. title: The Underrated Cadillac V-Sport Sedan V8 Fans Now Grab Cheap - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update Cadillac has long been known for V-power and sporty luxury prowess; it has turned out some of the best American sports sedans and coupes ever. However, in the past few years, there has been just one model on the lips of drivers looking for a Cadillac with some serious V8 grunt: the Blackwing. For everything the     Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing is good for, it is not a cheap sedan to buy, new or used. This is where this V-powered model comes in. If you can live with two fewer cylinders but still want a V engine and lower costs, this overlooked sedan gets the job done very well. The V8 is arguably the best engine configuration, but we are seeing less and less of them in the sports car market today. Yes, you get smooth power and lots of low-end torque, but for the most part, V8s have all but been replaced by smaller turbocharged engines and hybrid powertrains. Today, if you want a powerful V8 in a Cadillac sedan, you have to opt for a CT5-V Blackwing. That is no problem if you have a spare $98,900 for a 2026 model. However, alongside the Blackwing is one of the more affordable trims: the Cadillac CT5-V. The CT5-V is equipped with a high-output 3.0-liter bi-turbo LGY V6 paired with a ten-speed automatic transmission. Power is sent to the rear wheels as standard, but you can get used examples with all-wheel drive included. The dual turbos have electronic wastegates; SIDI provides precise fuel injection; variable displacement lubrication matches oil pressure to deliver the right amount of oil depending on engine speed; a DOHC and VVT are included; and thanks to the oversquare build (86 mm bore and 85.8 mm stroke), you get a very immediate throttle response across the rev range. First released in 2020, this V6-equipped sports sedan offers much of what the Blackwing does, but for less money. There may not be a supercharged V8 under the hood like in the Blackwing, but the 2020–2026 Cadillac CT5-V is still good for 360 horsepower at 5,400 rpm and a very healthy 405 pound-feet of torque at between 2,350 and 4,000 rpm. This translates to 0–60 mph times of 4.6 to 4.8 seconds, and a limited top speed of 156 mph. The Blackwing may well be the prized model of the CT5-V lineup, and it is the fastest, most powerful, and most capable on track, but the CT5-V still has a few tricks up its sleeve. There are currently (October 2026) 12 reviews on Kelley Blue Book, but all owners say they'd recommend buying one, and rate the CT5-V (not including the Blackwing) 4.9 out of 5 for performance, and 5 out of 5 for value, styling, reliability, and comfort. You could spend 2026 Blackwing money and get a six-speed manual transmission, an eLSD, Magnetic Ride Control 4.0,     Brembo brakes, 19-inch forged aluminum wheels, and Performance Traction Management (PTM), but if you look at what the 2020–2025 CT5-V gets, you may question spending so much. The CT5-V is one of the most athletic "lower trims" and gets Magnetic Ride Control with Gen-4 adaptive dampers, four-piston Brembo brakes, 19-inch wheels wrapped in Michelin Pilot Sport 4S tires, and the GM Alpha 2 platform. The Alpha 2 is the evolutionary step forward from the platform that underpins the sixth-generation Camaro and CTS, and it is the foundation that gives the CT5-V genuine handling prowess. You get a longitudinal front-engine layout, 50:50 weight distribution, a stiff chassis, a sport-tuned double-pivot MacPherson front strut, and a five-link independent rear setup. In short, it gets a lot of what you could want in a modern     sports sedan that is built to be driven. The most obvious distinction is the V8 that the Blackwing gets. The "real" Blackwing engine is a 4.2-liter bi-turbo V8 used in the CT6-V and CT6 Platinum, and is good for 550 horsepower and 640 pound-feet of torque. When Cadillac brought back the Blackwing name in 2022, it equipped the CT5-V Blackwing with a hand-built 6.2-liter supercharged pushrod V8 that produces 668 horsepower and 659 pound-feet of torque. A six-speed manual is standard, but a ten-speed automatic transmission is also available. The CT5-V cannot compete for outright speed; the Blackwing can reach 60 mph in as little as 3.4 seconds and top out at around 205 mph. If you want that kind of speed and the supercharged V8, though, it is going to cost you. According to Kelley Blue Book, the average used price for a 2022 Blackwing is $72,800; for a 2023 model, $76,600; for a 2024 model, $85,200; and for a one-year-old model, between $88,000 and $120,000. Also according to Kelley Blue Book, a 2020 CT5-V will cost you $33,200 on the used market; a 2021 model will cost you $35,400; and the 2022 model will cost you $39,500. A three-year-old CT5-V will set you back $44,300, while a two-year-old model has an average used price of $44,000, and a one-year-old model, around $57,000. The 2025 model is the first year of the refreshed CT5-V, hence the higher price. It comes with a high-res 33-inch touchscreen, new paint choices, more safety tech, and tweaked exterior features in the shape of a black mesh grille, black surrounds, a lower grille, and reshaped front air intakes. If you want a brand new one, it will cost you around $58,300. That is significantly less than the Blackwing, but the CT5-V still delivers considerable sporty capability. The CT5 is classed as a mid-sized luxury sedan, measuring in at 193.8 inches by 80.3 inches (with mirrors). This relatively big footprint allows for up to 42.4 inches of front legroom, 37.9 inches of rear legroom, and a decent trunk size of 11.9 cubic feet. However, if you want something smaller,     the CT4-V Blackwing still offers up to 10.7 cubic feet of storage space, up to 42.4 inches of front legroom, and 33.4 inches of rear legroom in a smaller package that measures in at 187.2 inches by 77.7 inches. You also get a far more powerful engine in the form of a 3.6-liter bi-turbo LF4 V6 that produces 472 horsepower at 5,750 rpm and 445 pound-feet of torque at 3,500 rpm. Thanks to the lighter weight, this translates to 0–60 mph times of between 3.9 and 4.1 seconds and a very direct feel, not to mention a more city-friendly size. To benefit from the Blackwing badge and as a very worthwhile alternative to both the CT5-V and Blackwing, a 2022 CT4-V Blackwing will cost you $49,400, a 2023 model will cost you $54,100, a 2024 model will cost you $51,700, and a 2025 model will cost you around ~$61,000. There is an obvious trade-off to not buying a Blackwing: you do not get a supercharged V8 under the hood. You also don't get the true Cadillac halo sports sedan. The Blackwing has somewhat resurrected the idea in the modern market that you can still have a powerful V8 in a usable, everyday package. The Blackwing is not the right choice if fuel economy is a priority; FuelEconomy.gov says it can achieve 15 combined mpg, and while the CT5-V is not much better at between 20 and 21 combined mpg, fuel economy is another factor to weigh against the much higher used prices of the Blackwing. The Blackwing is rightly the standout performer in the Cadillac lineup, but its new and used prices certainly reflect that. Its V8 niche, luxury interior standards, already-legendary nameplate, and genuine performance credentials have ensured prices will likely stay high for some time. A V6-equipped CT5-V may have two fewer cylinders and is slower, which is in part why it has been overlooked, but you can still reach 60 mph in less than 5 seconds, and it is still well-equipped for back roads and track days. That is, after all, what a     luxury sports sedan is made for. You still get a generous interior considering its performance capabilities, a lot of Blackwing-borrowed DNA, and, most importantly, an attractive used price for those who want performance without the premium. title: Revisiting State Responsibility in CAS Arbitration: Lessons from Semenya v Switzerland - Wolters Kluwer
content: Revisiting State Responsibility in CAS Arbitration: Lessons from Semenya v Switzerland The Court of Arbitration for Sport (“CAS”) is the final body for dispute resolution in international sports arbitration. However, CAS is a private body primarily governed by Swiss law (Article R45 of CAS Code). Its jurisdiction is based on arbitration clauses contained in contracts between parties. The international sporting ecosystem is also largely private, with most actors, including major sporting federations, operating as private legal entities. This has raised longstanding concerns that the private and arbitration-oriented structure of international sport does not adequately protect the human rights of athletes involved in sports disputes. These concerns have been partially mitigated by the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights (“ECtHR”), which has held in X and Y v The Netherlands that states have a positive obligation to ensure that private bodies within their jurisdiction comply with international human rights instruments, even where those instruments are not directly binding on the bodies themselves. CAS is located in Switzerland (Article R28 of CAS Code), a signatory to the European Convention on Human Rights (“ECHR” or “Convention”). Accordingly, Switzerland has a positive obligation to ensure that CAS complies with Convention standards, as confirmed by the ECtHR in Mutu & Pechstein v Switzerland (see here for the Blog’s previous coverage). However, determining which state bears this positive obligation is not straightforward. CAS is seated in Switzerland, meaning that the Swiss legal system is almost always implicated. At the same time, the parties to the dispute and the sporting bodies involved are often located in different jurisdictions, including states that are not parties to the ECHR. The question of which state is responsible for guaranteeing Convention rights in such situations has therefore remained uncertain. Previous coverage on the Blog has examined Semenya, including the Grand Chamber’s reasoning under Article 6(1), explaining the Court’s “particularly rigorous examination” standard and its implications for future cases (see here). Another post has considered whether this heightened standard is confined to sports arbitration or could also extend to commercial and other forms of voluntary arbitration, drawing comparisons with the CJEU’s judgment in RFC Seraing v FIFA (see here). This post, on the other hand, focuses on the question of state responsibility for CAS awards under the European Convention on Human Rights. Instead of examining how courts should review CAS awards, it asks which state should bear responsibility for a CAS award in the first place. It examines whether responsibility should depend on the place of arbitration or the location of the sporting body, an issue that has developed through the case law of both the CAS and the ECtHR. This post argues that the ECtHR’s 2025 judgment in Semenya v Switzerland (“Semenya”) clarifies this issue by distinguishing between procedural and substantive obligations within international sports arbitration. The judgment expressly confirms Switzerland’s responsibility for procedural Convention guarantees arising from its supervisory relationship with CAS arbitration. At the same time, by declining to attribute substantive responsibility for the underlying sporting regulations to Switzerland, the judgment narrows the possible location of substantive responsibility to the state in which the relevant sporting body is constituted and regulated. The post first discusses the two competing standards for determining state responsibility in sports arbitration: the place-of-arbitration standard and the place-of-sporting-body standard. It then examines how Semenya reconciles these standards. Competing Standards of State Responsibility in Sports Arbitration Over the years, courts have approached the question of state responsibility in sports arbitration through two competing standards. The first is the place-of-arbitration standard, under which responsibility lies with the state where the arbitration takes place. The second is the place-of-sporting-body standard, under which responsibility lies with the state where the relevant sporting federation is constituted and regulated. Consider the example of World Athletics, the international governing body for athletics, headquartered in Monaco. If an athlete alleges that World Athletics violated their human rights, but the arbitration is held before CAS in Switzerland, the two standards yield different outcomes. Under the place-of-arbitration standard, Switzerland would be responsible for ensuring compliance with Convention rights. Under the place-of-sporting-body standard, responsibility would instead lie with Monaco. The place-of-sporting-body standard first emerged in Pistorius v IAAF (2008). Oscar Pistorius, a double-amputee sprinter, challenged regulations issued by the International Association of Athletics Federations (“IAAF, now World Athletics”) that affected his eligibility to compete. The CAS panel declined to apply the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and its Optional Protocol (the “Disability Convention”) because Monaco, where the IAAF was headquartered, had not ratified the Disability Convention. The relevant question was therefore tied to the state’s legal obligations governing the federation, rather than to the arbitral seat. The IAAF was consequently treated as not being bound by the corresponding obligation. This approach appeared at the ECtHR level in Ali Rıza v Turkey (2020). The five applicants challenged the structural independence of the Turkish Football Federation's arbitration committee. The ECtHR found an Article 6 violation in relation to two applicants. The ECtHR held Turkey responsible for the Article 6 violation because the Turkish Football Federation was constituted and regulated under Turkish law. This remained the case even though the first applicant later pursued independent proceedings before CAS and the Swiss Federal Tribunal (“SFT”). The ECtHR located the source of the violation in the regulatory structure of the Turkish Football Federation. Alongside this, courts also developed the place-of-arbitration standard, under which Switzerland bears responsibility for CAS awards because CAS is seated in Lausanne and its awards are reviewable only by the SFT. This argument first emerged in Lazutina and Danilova v Switzerland. The applicants, two Russian cross-country skiers disqualified for doping, argued that the CAS award violated their human rights. They contended that Switzerland was responsible because the CAS award remained a private decision until the SFT upheld it, giving it legal effect under Swiss law. Switzerland, therefore, became responsible for any resulting violation, despite not being a party to the original dispute. Although the application was withdrawn before the ECtHR ruled on the merits, the same reasoning was later revived in Mutu and Pechstein v Switzerland. The standard was developed in NADA & KNSB v W. There, a CAS panel observed that although the direct applicability of the ECHR to private arbitration remained unsettled, Switzerland nevertheless bore indirect obligations because Swiss courts exercised supervisory jurisdiction over CAS proceedings. The ECtHR endorsed this reasoning in Mutu and Pechstein v Switzerland. The Court held that Switzerland’s responsibility was engaged because the SFT had dismissed the appeals against the CAS awards, thereby incorporating them into Swiss law. This was so even though Switzerland had no substantive connection to the underlying dispute. The same reasoning was subsequently reaffirmed in Platini v Switzerland. The SFT later confirmed, in a Turkish match-fixing dispute (4A_486/2019), that ECHR claims remained indirectly relevant through the doctrine of procedural public policy. The coexistence of these two standards left a central question unresolved in sports arbitration. It remained unclear whether state responsibility arose from procedural supervision of arbitration or from the fact that the relevant sporting federation created and imposed the underlying rules in the first place. As the next section argues, Semenya's reasoning significantly clarifies this ambiguity by separating procedural responsibility from substantive attribution. Procedural and Substantive Responsibility after Semenya The controversy in Semenya arose from challenges brought by South African athlete Caster Semenya against the Differences of Sex Development (“DSD”) Regulations, 2019, issued by World Athletics. Semenya argued that the regulations were discriminatory and violated her Convention rights. After unsuccessfully challenging the regulations before CAS and the SFT, she approached the ECtHR. The dispute resulted in both a 2023 Chamber judgment and a subsequent 2025 Grand Chamber judgment. The 2023 Chamber judgment created uncertainty about the basis for allocating Convention responsibility in sports arbitration. On the one hand, the Chamber found Switzerland’s Convention obligations engaged because the SFT had reviewed and validated the CAS award within the Swiss legal order. On the other hand, the Chamber stopped short of attributing the underlying DSD Regulations themselves to Switzerland. The judgment, therefore, appeared to engage both the place-of-arbitration and place-of-sporting-body standards without clearly distinguishing their respective roles. The 2025 Grand Chamber judgment can be read as clarifying this issue by drawing a clearer distinction between procedural responsibility and substantive responsibility. The Grand Chamber held that Switzerland’s obligations arose because CAS and the SFT formed part of a procedural framework operating within Swiss jurisdiction (paragraphs 104-105 of the judgment). Switzerland, therefore, bore responsibility for procedural Convention guarantees within the arbitral process, including effective judicial review, institutional independence, and meaningful scrutiny of arbitral outcomes (paragraph 201). At the same time, the Grand Chamber declined to attribute substantive responsibility for the DSD Regulations themselves to Switzerland (paragraph 80). Switzerland’s responsibility was instead confined to the adequacy of judicial protection available within the Swiss arbitral framework (paragraph 200). The logic behind the distinction is the existence of a sufficient jurisdictional nexus between the state and the relevant private actor. Under the ECtHR’s positive obligations framework, a state can only be expected to secure Convention compliance in relation to bodies operating within its jurisdictional and supervisory control. In Semenya, Switzerland possessed such a nexus in relation to CAS and the SFT, both of which operated within the Swiss legal order and were subject to Swiss supervisory authority. However, the Court did not treat Switzerland as exercising comparable control over World Athletics, a sporting federation constituted and regulated outside Switzerland. Read together, this reasoning implicitly clarifies the relationship between the two competing standards discussed earlier. The place where arbitration is conducted has sufficient jurisdictional nexus to ensure procedural rights arising from the arbitral process itself. However, that nexus does not necessarily extend to the substantive conduct of sporting federations whose regulations may give rise to the underlying rights violation. In such cases, the logic of the judgment points toward the state exercising regulatory authority over the relevant sporting federation as the more appropriate locus of substantive responsibility. While the Grand Chamber did not expressly endorse a place-of-sporting-body standard, its reasoning substantially narrows the possible basis on which substantive Convention responsibility may be allocated in future sports arbitration disputes. Semenya represents an important development in the relationship between international sports arbitration and the Convention system. The Grand Chamber expressly confirms Switzerland’s procedural obligations arising from its supervisory relationship with CAS arbitration. At the same time, by declining to attribute substantive responsibility for the underlying sporting regulations to Switzerland, the judgment reshapes the understanding of substantive responsibility within the Convention framework. Although the Court did not expressly adopt a place-of-sporting-body standard, its reasoning points strongly in that direction. Read in this way, Semenya introduces greater doctrinal coherence into sports arbitration while preserving meaningful human rights accountability within an increasingly transnational sporting order. ©2025 Wolters Kluwer N.V. and/or its subsidiaries. title: 25 years on: Beckham v Greece - England Football | Home
content: On 6 October 2001, at Old Trafford, David Beckham scored one of them. The Three Lions’ FIFA World Cup 2002 qualifier against Greece was already a highly charged match-up. Sven-Göran Eriksson's side knew a victory would guarantee top spot in Group 9, but with Germany also dropping points against Finland, a draw would be enough to seal their place at the tournament. A defeat, on the other hand, would mean the play-offs. David Beckham scores a memorable free-kick at Old Trafford against Greece to secure England's World Cup place Greece twice took the lead, first through Angelos Charisteas before Teddy Sheringham levelled for England shortly after coming off the bench. When Nikolaidis restored the visitors' advantage in the 69th minute, the pressure was suddenly immense. England were running out of time and, as the minutes ticked away, Sheringham was fouled and the set-piece was in Beckham territory. “Will Beckham have another attempt at goal?” asked the commentator, with the Three Lions trailing 2-1. “Beckham could raise the roof here, with a goal.” Up stepped Beckham, striking the ball perfectly as his free-kick curled over the wall and beyond the reach of Greek goalkeeper Antonios Nikopolidis. “I don’t believe it,” was the cry from the commentary box, with England seconds away from booking their place at the World Cup. “David Beckham scores the goal to take England all the way to the World Cup Finals. Give that man a knighthood!” As it happened, he was knighted later down the line, in 2025, and that goal against Greece was immortalised. “I remember putting the ball down and Teddy [Sheringham] kind of came over and nudged me out of the way,” recalled Beckham, speaking previously on that famous goal. “Me and Teddy were really good friends. He said, ‘I’ll take this one’. I said ‘it’s too far for you’. “I remember hearing the band – the beat of the drum in the back of my mind. Then everything went quiet.
