title: Makovac and Latin v. Slovenia - ECHR
content: Fair trial rights in proceedings concerning fines for fishing in Slovenian waters In the case of Makovac and Latin v. Slovenia the Court held that there had been no violation of the right to a fair trial in respect of the first applicant and that there had been a violation in respect of the second applicant. The case concerned Croatian commercial fishing workers’ complaints about the proceedings concerning fines against them for illegally entering and fishing in Slovenian waters. They argued that there had been a breach of their defence rights in the minor offence proceedings against them, in particular that there had been no hearings in their cases. The ECHR found that it had been legitimate for the Slovenian courts to do without an oral hearing to convict first applicant. Her conviction had been based on, among other things, photographs with two recognisable individuals which she could have challenged. Second applicant’s conviction had, however, been based on his being identified by a fisheries inspector and unspecified social media posts. An oral hearing would have been essential to put that evidence to the test.

title: The Arguments We Did and Didn’t Hear in Suncor v. Boulder - Legal Planet
content: The Supreme Court heard oral arguments today in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. At issue is whether the city and county of Boulder can move forward with its state court case against defendants Exxon Mobil Corporation and Suncor Energy for allegedly deceiving the public about their products’ role in climate change. Some three dozen local governments and states throughout the United States have filed similar lawsuits in state court against fossil fuel companies over their alleged deception and false advertising. Although none of these cases have yet gone to trial, the U.S. Supreme Court decided to review Boulder’s case at the request of the oil company petitioners. There is much to unpack about the arguments and how the justices received them. But I first want to highlight an argument that went largely unmade, one that may matter as the justices decide the case. (You can read or hear the arguments at the court’s website.) Several justices pressed the idea that a tort suit is regulation by another name. Justice Barrett put it most directly: “Everybody agrees that state tort law is a form of regulation.” Justice Kavanaugh warned that suits like Boulder’s could “bankrupt” defendants. Chief Justice Roberts asked whether the suit was “an attempt to evade” the Court’s precedents on emissions. Boulder’s counsel answered that a damages award doesn’t prohibit anything; it just requires defendants “to internalize a portion of the cost of their activities.” That is true. But it invites a response the Court has given before: damages regulate conduct too. There’s another answer: The Supreme Court has always recognized that tort verdicts influence behavior, and it has never treated that as a reason to wipe out state remedies Congress chose to preserve. That’s why, as I told Mother Jones in a preview article, it’s useful to see Suncor as a tort case rather than as a climate lawsuit. From nuclear power to tobacco to pesticides, the Court has held that federal regulation and state compensation can coexist. I’ll expound on my reasoning below. First, let’s turn to what was actually argued. The oil companies’ broadest theory had a bad day, but narrower ones are very much alive. Several justices resisted the idea that the Constitution’s structure alone bars state climate suits. Justice Kagan asked of the companies’ “plan of the Convention” theory: “Where’s the text for that? Where’s the support for that? Where’s the precedent for that? Where’s the anything for that?” Justice Barrett called the companies’ retreat to constitutional structure “a little slippery.” Justices Gorsuch, Sotomayor, and Jackson also pressed hard on it. The first was Justice Kavanaugh’s. In his view, four precedents (Milwaukee I, Milwaukee II, International Paper Co. v. Ouellette, and American Electric Power v. Connecticut, or AEP) make “crystal-clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law unless Congress specifically preserves state law.” On that reading, the Clean Air Act preserves suits under the law of the state where the pollution originates (the “source state”). It does not preserve suits under the law of the injured state, like Colorado. When petitioners’ counsel pointed out that Boulder is relying on Colorado law, Kavanaugh replied, “That resolves this case.” The second was Justice Kagan’s. She pointed to AEP’s closing paragraph, which says that whether a state suit is available depends on the preemptive effect of the Clean Air Act. That makes this an ordinary question of statutory preemption, not constitutional structure. But Kagan also suggested to Boulder’s counsel that the Clean Air Act might be “the more natural and simpler route towards [the companies’] view of what should happen here.” So, both narrower routes could still limit the options for Boulder. The open question is how much of the case survives. It’s worth noting that the foreign-affairs framing that dominated op-ed pages in the lead-up to argument drew no questions from the justices. It came up only in petitioners’ opening and, briefly, in rebuttal. So, what can we tell from the questions each justice asked? Justices Sotomayor and Jackson: seem firmly with Boulder. Sotomayor: (1) noted the companies hadn’t raised their extraterritoriality argument below until their reply brief; (2) questioned the Court’s jurisdiction, and asked whether it should certify the question of Colorado procedure to the Colorado Supreme Court rather than decide it; (3) said she didn’t know that “we’ve ever talked of spending money on litigation as a constitutional injury”; (4) told Boulder’s counsel that this case looks like Commonwealth Edison v. Montana, which upheld a state coal tax despite the Clean Air Act: “Isn’t this your case?” Jackson called the case premature, noting the companies’ other federal defenses are still pending in state court. She said the companies’ extraterritoriality test “seems very close to a causation standard” and asked why they were trying to “constitutionalize” it. She also asked the Principal Deputy Solicitor General, Sarah Harris, whether Colorado, home to Suncor’s refineries, is itself a source state. That question matters, because Ouellette preserves source-state law. Justice Kavanaugh: firmly with the oil companies. He nearly coached the Solicitor General’s office toward a stronger argument: interstate pollution is federal unless Congress preserves state law, so why wasn’t that the lead? He answered Kagan’s tobacco-and-opioids question by saying air and water pollution are different. He asked why a tort suit should be treated differently from a state statute doing the same thing. He closed by quoting AEP’s line that an expert agency is better equipped than “individual district judges” to address climate change, and asked whether the same isn’t true of “a six-person state jury in Boulder.” Justice Barrett: leaning toward the companies, but by a narrower route. She rejected the companies’ constitutional-structure theory. She read the Clean Air Act’s savings clauses as preserving, not authorizing, preexisting state authority: “It says ‘preserve.’ And a saving clause suggests that you’re saving something that already exists.” But she described that preexisting state authority as “much more circumscribed.” She agreed the Clean Air Act did not make state law “spring into effect.” And she embraced Kavanaugh’s framing: “I think Justice Kavanaugh is right. It’s also simply in our precedent. We’ve called it an enclave of federal common law.” To Boulder, she posed a hypothetical Colorado statute capping emissions in the other 49 states. When Boulder’s counsel agreed such a statute would be invalid, she asked: “So, the same thing can happen through the tort suit, though?” Barrett also raised EPA’s recent position that the Clean Air Act does not authorize regulating greenhouse gases from motor vehicles. Her point was not that this helps Boulder. If the Act no longer displaces federal common law, she suggested, the issue reverts to federal common law, and a federal court could decide there is no cause of action. She seems prepared to rule for the companies without their constitutional theory. Justice Kagan: with Boulder on method, uncertain on outcome. She pressed the companies hardest. She noted the suit resembles the 1990s tobacco suits and the more recent opioid litigation: “This is chapter 3. So, if this is chapter 3, were chapters 1 and 2 also preempted?” She added that the companies may have a weaker claim on the merits, “but this is the same kind of lawsuit against the same kind of actors for the same kind of harm.” She also challenged the constitutional theory and pointed to AEP’s closing paragraph. With Boulder’s counsel, though, she asked: “You really read Milwaukee I to allow state regulation of air and water to any significant degree?” She also said Boulder’s suits “are so related to what kinds of emissions are appropriate.” When Boulder’s counsel argued that EPA’s disclaimer of authority makes Clean Air Act preemption hard to decide, she replied that “the statute is the statute.” Her tobacco analogy suggests sympathy for the deception claims. Her Clean Air Act questions suggest skepticism about claims based on production and emissions. One shouldn’t count her as a vote to keep every claim. Justice Gorsuch: seems skeptical of the companies’ theory, but hard to read. His Texas hypothetical exposed a gap in petitioners’ logic: they would object even to Texas law applied to a Texas source. He then pressed the Solicitor General’s office. EPA, he noted, has disclaimed the power to regulate greenhouse gases “not just from motor vehicles but more recently from stationary sources too.” If the Clean Air Act displaced federal common law and state law is also barred, “nobody can sue at all?” Harris answered, “I think that’s correct.” That skepticism fits Gorsuch’s opinions in National Pork Producers v. Ross and Virginia Uranium. He asked Boulder’s counsel whether this is “the same thing as the classic car manufacturer case.” Chief Justice Roberts: seems skeptical of both sides, and harder on Boulder by the end. He pressed petitioners’ counsel with an ordinary tort hypothetical: if you throw a rock over the border and hit someone, you can be sued there. He told the Solicitor General’s office that familiar mass-tort and internet cases seem to be “precisely what’s going on here.” But with Boulder’s counsel, he raised the prospect of municipalities in every state copying Boulder’s pleadings. He then asked, “isn’t your suit an attempt to evade those decisions? It’s really … an effort to reduce emissions.” Justice Thomas: uncertain but may be leaning toward the companies on the merits. He opened both petitioners’ and the government’s arguments by asking about jurisdiction, but he often opens that way, so I wouldn’t read much into it. More telling, he asked Boulder’s counsel whether anything limits whom plaintiffs can sue, including large retailers. Counsel acknowledged, “Nothing in our theory prevents that.” Since our previous Legal Planet Guide offered possible outcomes—always speculative, of course—here’s how it looks after oral arguments, roughly from most to least likely: As I said at the outset, Justice Barrett is right in one sense: “everybody agrees” tort law regulates, even if it is intended to address actual harms not addressed by statutes. However, the Court has never treated a tort remedy’s regulatory effect, by itself, as a reason to preempt it. Here’s my reasoning: That’s my take. What did you think? Share in the comments. title: Joyce V. Frederick - Rutland Herald
content:
Clear skies. Scattered frost possible. Low 33F. Winds light and variable.. Clear skies. Scattered frost possible. Low 33F. Winds light and variable. Joyce V. Frederick WALLINGFORD — Joyce V. Frederick, 59, of Wallingford, passed away peacefully on Thursday, October 1st, at Rutland Regional Medical Center after a courageous battle with breast cancer. She is leaving behind a legacy of love, faith, and a reminder to all of us to never stay seated when life gives us the chance to move. She was born on August 6, 1967, in Rutland, VT, the daughter of Louis and Joyce Frederick. Ms. Frederick attended North Clarendon Elementary, Mill River Union High School, and Community College of Vermont. For many years, Ms. Frederick worked at the BROC community food shelf in Rutland. She was driven by a deep love for helping others; she was a dedicated community member who found immense joy in connecting with people and bringing comfort to those going through difficult times. Ms. Frederick was happiest when she was on her feet, organizing donations and greeting everyone with a warm smile. She never met a stranger and had a beautiful way of making everyone feel seen, welcomed, and loved. She had a rare, effortless warmth that drew people in, turning brief encounters into lasting connections. She loved lounging by a wood stove with a good book alongside her precious dogs, attending basket raffles, thrift shopping, hiking in the great outdoors, and her best friend James Cote. She is survived by her loving family, including her son David Frederick (Aletia Frederick) of Granville, NY, daughter Jessica Souza (Justin Souza), grandchildren Juliana and Jordan Souza of Richmond Hill, GA. brothers Wilbur Frederick (Debbie Frederick) and Ira Frederick (Beth Sheehe-Blaisdell), sisters Marie Regimbald (Howard Regimbald), Cindy Majka (Dick Majka), Doreen Hussey, and Tina Frederick (Art Depalma). As well as her beloved nieces and nephews, many friends, co-workers, and countless individuals in the community whose lives she touched and changed for the better. She is reunited in peace with her parents, Louis and Joyce Frederick, nieces Alyssa Frederick and Heather Hunt, and nephew Rick Hunt. A future burial service will be held for family and close friends, followed by a Celebration of Life. title: Read the Bold Print: What Palazzo v. Bayview Means for Bankruptcy Disclaimers - JDSupra
content:
Once a debtor files a bankruptcy petition, the stay kicks in and collection activity must grind to a halt to avoid exposing the creditor to liability. While the automatic stay prohibits creditors from attempting to collect on a debt, the stay does not eliminate the need to communicate altogether. Creditors typically still need to send certain account statements or provide other pertinent documents to a debtor about their account. But what should the creditor do when certain notifications may be in direct contravention of the automatic stay of the Bankruptcy Code? The Fourth Circuit’s recent decision in Palazzo v. Bayview Loan Servicing, LLC, provides welcome clarity. The court held that sending certain statements and communications will not violate the automatic stay, provided the appropriate disclaimers are included. Ruben Palazzo filed a Chapter 13 bankruptcy petition in February 2016, to reorganize his debts. During his bankruptcy, his mortgage servicers continued sending him monthly account statements and 1098 tax forms, along with payoff statements that Palazzo had personally requested. Palazzo sued, alleging that those communications were efforts to collect on a debt which are prohibited by the automatic stay and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA). The district court ultimately sided with the mortgage servicer, which was upheld on appeal. The Court scrutinized the specific language in each of the communications. The Monthly Statements and Payoff Statements each provided a breakdown of the outstanding balance, the current interest rate, and other fees and amounts that would become due after the bankruptcy concluded. Critically, each statement included a prominent bankruptcy disclaimer that expressly notified the debtor that the statement was being sent “for informational and compliance purposes only” and that they were “not an attempt to collect a debt against [the debtor].” The Court found that the disclaimers were “clear and unequivocal,” and that a reasonable reader in Palazzo’s position would have understood that no payment was being demanded.  More importantly, Palazzo himself had requested the payoff statements, which undercut his argument that they were sent as an attempt to collect on a debt, rather than a ministerial response to his inquiry. The 1098 tax statements similarly contained information about the interest paid and remaining principal for tax purposes. While those statements did not contain any specific disclaimers, the Court held that they were clearly being sent to provide information to a debtor, necessary for him to complete his taxes. Because of that, the Court found that providing those forms did not evidence an intent to collect. The Palazzo decision confirms what careful creditors have long practiced, and it offers a blueprint for anyone who needs to communicate with a bankrupt debtor. Should a debtor allege a stay violation based on routine correspondence, the Palazzo framework provides a strong defense—so long as your communications contained proper disclaimers and did not demand payment. But be careful not to become complacent and treat all communications similarly. As noted, the Court paid particular attention to the exact wording of the disclaimers provided, and the facts surrounding those communications. As a result, careful drafting of form communications and periodic review of disclaimer language is important to ensure that there is no inadvertent violation of the automatic stay. Consult your attorney before sending notices to debtors who are in a pending bankruptcy proceeding or have received a discharge. title: Challenges and Solutions in Oligonucleotide Analysis, Part V: Troubles with Phosphorothioate Oligonucleotides - Chromatography Online
content: "LC Troubleshooting" explores why phosphorothioate oligonucleotides (ONs) diastereomers challenge liquid chromatography. In this article, we focus on analysis of phosphorothioate oligonucleotides (ONs). Thiolation of the phosphate backbone of an ON forms diastereomers that complicate their analysis. We describe recent advances in the separation and characterization of phosphorothioate oligonucleotides by liquid chromatography and ion mobility mass spectrometry. The recent expansion of pharmaceutical portfolios to include more therapeutic oligonucleotides (ONs) has led to a dramatic increase in research of chromatographic methods for analysis and purification of these molecules. This has been accompanied by a new set of method development and troubleshooting challenges, particularly for those whose background has been focused on small molecule separations, which have not previously been addressed in any detail in the “LC Troubleshooting” column. Thus, I am thrilled to have Martin Gilar join me for a series of LC Troubleshooting installments focused on challenges encountered in liquid chromatography (LC) analyses of ONs. Gilar is one of the world’s experts on this topic, and this series of articles should be a rich resource for LC practitioners working in this area. In Part I of this series, we outlined liquid chromatography (LC) methods for oligonucleotide (ON) analysis;1 in Part II, we elaborated the principles of ion-pairing reversed-phase LC (IPRP-LC);2 in Part III, we focused on LC-mass spectrometry (MS);3 and in Part IV we highlighted some of the less-known challenges of oligonucleotide analysis, such as nonspecific adsorption, peak splitting, and others.4 In Part V, we explain the reasons why analysis of phosphorothioate (PS) oligonucleotides is more complicated, and why the separation of PS diastereomers is becoming more important for oligonucleotide drug development. Figure 1 illustrates the structures of the two diastereomers of a single phosphorothioate linkage in the backbone of an ON molecule. Oligonucleotide synthesis uses mononucleotide building blocks consisting of pentoses with chiral carbons (carbons 1, 3, and 4 in DNA or 1, 2, 3, and 4 in RNA molecules; carbon numbers are shown in Figure 1). Replacement of one of the oxygens in the phosphate group linking two pentoses with a sulfur converts the achiral phosphodiester group to a phosphorothioate group and creates a new chiral center. The addition of this chiral phosphate group to a stereochemically pure ON molecule yields Sp and Rp stereoisomers (Figure 1), which are not enantiomers (because they are not mirror images), but diastereomers. The number of diastereomers (Z) in the ON increases with the number of PS linkages (n) according to formula Z = 2n. In other words, the isomeric complexity of the ON increases exponentially as the number of PS groups increases. One, two, three, or 24 PS linkages will produce two, four, eight, or 16.8 million diastereomers! Figure 1. Structures of two phosphorothioate diastereomers of DNA. The first generation of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapeutic compounds relied on full phosphorothioation of the ON backbone to improve the ASO resistance against exo- and endonucleases in vivo.5,6 The properties and utility of PS oligonucleotides for therapeutic applications were studied and reviewed by Eckstein and others.7–13 Both Sp and Rp forms (Figure 1) are more resistant to enzymatic hydrolysis, but the Sp isomer is exceptionally resistant to exonucleases, and the Rp isomer against endonucleases.10 Stereochemistry of PS linkages also affects hybridization strength with complementary ONs: Rp forms hybridize with greater stability resulting in higher melting temperatures than Sp forms.13,14 While the first and second generations of ASO compounds were heavily PS modified, recent therapeutic oligonucleotides use 2’ fluorination or 2’ O-methylation (among others) to maintain in vivo stability and use PS modifications less extensively.15–17 Typically, one or two PS modifications protect 5’ and/or 3’ termini of small interfering RNA (siRNA) or guide RNA (gRNA) therapeutic molecules.18 Stereopure PS oligonucleotides were also proposed for therapeutic purposes, containing either only Sp or Rp PS linkages.14,19 It has been reported that PS oligonucleotide synthesis does not yield a 50:50 ratio of Sp:Rp diastereomers (as is the case for achiral synthesis of enantiomers);11,12 different nucleotide coupling activators used for synthesis produce different yields of Rp:Sp linkages. The ability to characterize diastereomeric composition of PS ONs has been requested by regulatory agencies, prompting studies aimed at assessing the equivalency of therapeutic PS ONs.13,20 It is known that achiral columns exhibit selectivity for diastereomers of PS ONs—that is, stationary phases such as C18 (that don’t explicitly have chiral characteristics), can chromatographically resolve diastereomers.18,21 While this is obviously beneficial in cases where separation of the diastereomers is desirable, it also means that LC analyses of PS ON samples consisting of thousands-to-millions of diastereomers exhibit wider peaks compared to phosphodiester ONs of the same sequence (that is, no PS linkages)22–24 or to stereochemically pure PS ONs.14 The partial separation of PS diastereomers (which leads to peak broadening) makes it more challenging to resolve ON metabolites or truncation products carried over from the synthesis of the parent PS ON.25 Several strategies were proposed to suppress the separation of PS diastereomers, thereby reducing this “chemical” source of peak broadening. These include the addition of hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP) to IPRP mobile phases,24,25 the use of hydrophobic ion-pairing (IP) reagents,23 and elevated column temperatures.22 The effect of ion-pairing reagent hydrophobicity on diastereomeric separation in IPRP-LC is illustrated in Figure 2. Figure 2. (a) Separation of 21nt ONs of the same sequence, but with different numbers of PS modifications (shown as asterisks in the figure). PS modifications were placed on 5’- and 3’-termini, or in the center of the sequence. Chromatographic conditions: Column: Pre-mier BEH C18 columns, 50 × 2.1 mm, 1.7 μm; flow rate: 0.4 mL/min; temperature: 60 °C; gradient elution with a slope of 1% acetonitrile/min. The mobile phase composition was chosen as the starting point so that peaks eluted over similar time windows in each case. The 100 mM ammonium acetate (AmAc) buffer enables the separation of diastereomers with the exception of ON 1 (no isomers present). Partial isomeric separation is observed in 100 mM TEAA buffer; overlapping isomers form broad peaks for ONs 4 and 5. 100-mM diisopropylethylamine acetate (DIPPA) ion-pairing mobile phase system suppresses dias-tereomeric separation more effectively. (b) Separation of 6nt ON with 4 PS modifications. Conditions are the same as in (a), except that 25 mM ammonium acetate buffer was used. Partial separation is achieved with 13 peaks observed for the 16 diastereomers present in the sample. Chromatograms in Figure 2a were adapted from reference 23. Diisopropylethylamine acetate is more efficient in suppressing diastereomeric separation of PS ONs than triethylammonium acetate (TEAA) and thus provides narrower peaks in IPRP LC. Similar results were observed for dibutylamine or hexylamine ion-pairing systems.23 An ion-pairing mobile phase system consisting of 5 mM tributylammonium acetate is also highly effective for suppression of diastereomeric resolution and often used for LC–MS analysis of PS ONs.20,26 For ON drugs containing a limited number of PS modifications (1–4 PS linkages), it is feasible to resolve the modest number of diastereomers. It has been shown that 2–16 isomers can be resolved with reversed-phase liquid chromatography (RPLC),12,25 anion-exchange LC,18,27 or other methods.17,28 Diastereomeric characterization of PS ONs is an active research subject of several research groups.17,21,26,29–33 Figure 2b illustrates that RPLC is an efficient method for the separation of diastereomers; however, the resolution success in RPLC (and with hydrophilic ion-pairing systems) strongly depends on the ON sequence motif.11,12,34 PS ON sequences consisting of C and G nucleotides are better resolved than motifs consisting of A or U nucleotides; chemical modification (2’F, 2’OMe or nucleotides such as locked nucleic acid, LNA) often enhances the diastereomeric separation, but not always.34 Despite the volume of current research, the LC separation of these diastereomers remains poorly understood, and difficult to predict. Available reports suggest that successful separation of PS ONs is achievable up to 16 diastereomers, especially for 4–6 nt-long oligonucleotides.18,33 However, chromatographic resolution is incomplete for longer oligonucleotides with more than four PS modifications, and not feasible for samples of fully thiolated ONs that contain thousands to millions of diastereomers. Roussis and colleagues developed chromatographic methods that enable relative estimation of diastereomeric distributions in PS oligonucleotides from the chromatographic peak retention shift. For example, under RPLC conditions, Sp species are more strongly retained than Rp diastereomers.10–12,14 They showed that the retention shift pattern clearly differentiates between six model diastereoisomeric mixtures (of the same ON sequence) using several chromatographic methods and 31P nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.20,35 In an alternative approach, PS oligonucleotides were fragmented via chemical31 or enzymatic cleavage,29 or by MS/MS fragmentation, followed by ion mobility spectrometry (IMS) separation of the resulting 2-5 nt-long species.36 It has been shown that the IMS method (separating charged molecules in the gas phase due to their different collisional cross-sections) provides useful diastereomeric resolution of 2-5 nt PS ON diastereomers. Separation was achieved with high-resolution ion mobility coupled with HRMS30 or with cyclic IMS.37 Good agreement between IMS and IPRP LC results were reported36 for ONs up to 5 nt, containing two PS linkages (four diastereomers, Figure 3). The encouraging IMS capabilities for analysis of PS diastereomers will undoubtedly be further explored, optimizing the selection of charged ions, and conditions for best IMS resolution. Figure 3. IPRP LC (a) and ion mobility spectom (b) analysis of a model 5nt C*U*CGA ON, where the asterisk denotes the position of PS linkage. Total ion current MS detection was used in IPRP- LC to monitor the separation of four diastereomers. (b) displays IMS distribu-tions for the -2-charge state. Note that IMS ion arrival time and IPRP LC retention time are not correlated. Figure adapted from reference 36. Thiolation of the backbone of therapeutic oligonucleotides is a common and useful modification that enhances their in vivo stability. Molecules with the specific Sp and Rp stereo configurations exhibit distinct biochemical activities, such as differences in resistance to nuclease enzymes, and different energies of hybridization with complementary ON sequences. However, this modification also presents challenges when analyzing these molecules using liquid chromatography. Thiolation leads to the formation of diastereomers due to newly formed chiral centers, which can in turn lead to a kind of chemical peak broadening due to partial separation of numerous diastereomers. In this installment of “LC Troubleshooting,” we’ve highlighted some of the difficulties encountered in the analysis of PS ONs by LC, and reviewed strategies that can be used when characterization of the diastereomeric composition of an ON sample is needed. Although there has been tremendous progress in this area recently, further research and development of LC and MS (IMS) methodologies are still needed to make the characterization of PS diastereomers more robust, explainable, and predictable. title: LCV Statement on SCOTUS Oral Arguments in Suncor v. Boulder - League of Conservation Voters
content: Washington, D.C. — In response to today’s oral arguments at the Supreme Court in Suncor v. Boulder, the League of Conservation Voters (LCV) issued the following statement from Senior Director of Judiciary and Democracy Doug Lindner: “Big Polluters have padded their profits by fueling the climate crisis and lying to the public for decades while our families get sicker and our communities bear the costs of more and worse climate disasters. Suncor v. Boulder is about whether they’ll get away with it. Communities across the country are working to hold them accountable in court, but the Big Polluters are asking their friends on the Supreme Court — as well as their friends in Congress and the Trump administration — to protect them from accountability. Like Trump, the MAGA justices on the Supreme Court have long helped fossil fuel CEOs grow richer as people pay the price for pollution, wildfires, and drought-induced water shortages. Even with Samuel Alito recused, five other MAGA justices have similar records of choosing polluters over the people and the law. Americans deserve judges and justices we can trust to deliver equal justice under law. We need Congress to act on Supreme Court structural and ethical reform, and until then, we need our Senators to block pro-polluter nominees for the federal bench.”

title: State of Florida v. Scott Glenn Knowlton II - 7th Judicial Circuit State Attorney's Office
content: Volusia County Defendant Sentenced to 45 Years in Prison for Violating Probation DAYTONA BEACH – During a hearing on Monday, Volusia County defendant Scott Knowlton was sentenced to 45 years in prison. In July, he admitted to violating the conditions of his probation 14 times. Knowlton was convicted in 2023 of Trafficking in Fentanyl (14 grams to 28 grams), Possession of Methamphetamine with Intent to Sell, Possession of Cocaine with Intent to Sell and Grand Theft of a Motor Vehicle, along with two other felonies and a misdemeanor. He served time in prison for those offenses before being released and placed on probation. While on probation in August 2025, Knowlton ran away from a Holly Hill police officer. He dropped a backpack containing fentanyl and other drug paraphernalia. Once he was identified, a warrant was issued for his arrest. Knowlton remained wanted when Volusia County Sheriff’s Office Chief Deputy Brian Henderson encountered him in Daytona Beach in November 2025. The incident led to additional charges, including Kidnap Inflict Bodily Harm/Terrorize Victim, Battery, Resisting an Officer Without Violence, Carrying a Concealed Weapon by In-State Felon and Possession of Paraphernalia. As he was driving down Atlantic Avenue, Chief Deputy Henderson witnessed Knowlton chasing a woman who appeared afraid of him. When she tried to run away, Knowlton grabbed and pulled her away against her will. Henderson intervened and told Knowlton to stop, but he ignored the command, dropped a backpack and ran away toward the Ocean Center. Surveillance video later showed Knowlton punching the woman in the back of the head and continuing to hold her as she tried to escape. Deputies also recovered a gun and drug paraphernalia from the backpack Knowlton left at the scene. The victim was treated at the scene for her injuries. Two days later, Knowlton was found and arrested in Ormond Beach. “This defendant was irredeemable – a lost cause who was never going to change,” State Attorney R.J. Larizza said. “Good riddance.” “Last time I saw Scott Knowlton, he was assaulting and dragging his girlfriend in the street,” Chief Deputy Brian Henderson recalled. “Today, it was a pleasure to see him held accountable and sentenced to prison where he can’t hurt anyone else. Violent, repeat criminals like him are a danger to our community and a drain on society.” Volusia Sheriff Mike Chitwood added a thank you to the anonymous tipster who turned Knowlton in after a reward was posted. The defendant has additional charges related to the drug and domestic violence cases pending in Volusia County. The Violation of Probation case was investigated by the Volusia Sheriff’s Office. Assistant State Attorney Ashley McCarthy successfully prosecuted the case for the State of Florida. The Honorable Leah Case heard the case and imposed sentence. title: Grand openings: what four introductions in Suncor v. Boulder show about starting a brief - SCOTUSblog
content: When the court opens its term on Monday with the blockbuster case Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, the justices will have digested four principal briefs. They are Suncor Energy and the other energy companies’ opening brief (Kannon Shanmugam), the United States’ amicus brief supporting the energy companies (Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris), Boulder’s brief (Kevin Russell), and the energy companies’ reply. The merits question is whether federal law bars state-law claims for injuries attributed to interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions. But this post is for anyone who writes briefs, in the Supreme Court or in any court, and it is about the introduction: the prime real estate that offers the court a frame for all the law and facts to follow. Each introduction combines, in its own recipe, the four techniques I outline in my book on legal advocacy, “Point Made”: Brass Tacks, the narrative lens explaining “who, what, when, where, why, how.” The Short List, the logical lens numbering your path to victory. Why Should I Care?, the pragmatic lens giving the court a reason to want to find for you. And Flashpoint, the contrasting lens drawing a line in the sand. The way each side navigates these introductions, each under 1,000 words, also reveals what it sees as its strengths and weaknesses. Even, or especially, when the legal issues are abstract, the best introductions spin a narrative line showing how the parties reached an impasse and how the court should guide them out of it. Call it a Tale of Four Briefs. What story does each tell? For the energy companies: A city and a county in Colorado have sued “two of the world’s countless fossil-fuel producers” for local harms at the end of a global chain, in which production and marketing “resulted in consumers’ use of fossil fuels around the world, which released . . . emissions, which combined with all other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere to alter the global climate, which then resulted in localized physical harms in Boulder.” There’s the causal chain in one sentence. For the government: A single city wants the law of a single state to dictate how the world addresses a global problem: by penalizing conduct “outside Colorado,” much of it “entirely overseas,” for harms in Boulder “from wildfire damage to public-health costs.” The introduction also issues a verdict on this tale: “Absolutely not.” For Boulder: Petitioners “have run to this Court at the case’s outset” to ask for a rule that Congress, not courts, should make. The case is “far from final judgment,” and the Colorado Supreme Court has not yet decided whether respondents have stated a claim under state law. It’s a procedural tale of when and why, but with no concrete narrative of local injuries: Boulder never appears, and Colorado appears only in the name of its highest court. Recounting the injury tale would mean tracing the energy companies’ causal chain; the procedural opening keeps the focus instead on institutional authority and timing. For the energy companies’ reply: Four sentences recast the energy companies’ account of who, what, and why as propositions that, the reply says, Boulder “do[es] not dispute.” That is Brass Tacks used to pull the court back to the energy companies’ story – and to ask the court to treat its factual premises as common ground so that the fight is over their legal effects. The Short List consists of the three or four points you would make to a judge who gave you only 60 seconds to speak. The points must also work as a unit: what does each of these promise, and do they relate to one another as rungs (each a fallback for the one above), gates (reasons the court can abstain from action), or axes (independent grounds that add up)? Here is how I would distill each introduction’s path to victory. (By “introduction” I mean each brief’s opening overview, labeled or not.) The energy companies’ opening brief: rungs on a ladder, all resting on one premise – that the claims target interstate and international emissions Boulder: gates, loosely speaking, united by restraint (who decides, when, and by what method) The energy companies’ reply: the opening list, restructured and reinforced Why Should I Care? Give the court a reason to want to find for you This technique gives the court a reason to feel good about finding for you, usually by triggering one of three judicial fears if it were to decide the other way: misconstruing a doctrine or statute; creating new duties, rules, or defenses; or reaching an unfair result or causing harm. Gauge this part of the introduction by the anxiety it triggers or relieves. The energy companies’ opening brief: an unfair result and harm, at national scale, without naming petitioner ExxonMobil in the introduction, which keeps attention on harm to others rather than on the petitioners themselves The government: harm to the federal system, tested through a hypothetical Boulder: misconstruing a doctrine and creating a new rule, a matter of method rather than scale The reply: the opening brief’s scale argument, compressed into two images Notice, too, that Boulder does not foreground residents’ injuries in the introduction. Rather, Boulder includes those harms at the start of the opening statement instead. The effect is to keep the opening focused on institutional authority and procedural restraint rather than on the causal chain that the energy companies emphasize. A Flashpoint draws a line in the sand between two competing views of the dispute so that you can preempt your opponent’s attempts to make the case into something it’s not. The energy companies’ opening brief: scale, global against local, which makes the suit itself sound unprecedented The energy companies make the state-tort litigation sound novel and the principles barring it settled. Boulder makes the state-law remedies sound ordinary and the proposed bar novel. Both sides want the same advantage: to make the other side explain why the court should depart from familiar ground. Before you file, ask whether your introduction does the same. Ross Guberman is the president of Legal Writing Pro LLC and the founder of BriefCatch LLC. title: Alaska Policy Forum v. Alaska Public Offices Commission - Cato Institute
content: Because Alaska’s decision to treat public policy analysis as campaign speech triggers duties of registration, reporting, and donor disclosure, it is incompatible with the guarantees of the First Amendment. Learn more about Cato’s Amicus Briefs Program. Cato’s latest amicus brief serves to defend the First Amendment interests of an Alaska think tank that regularly opines on matters of public policy. The ability to participate in the marketplace of ideas and express views on such matters should not require mastery of arcane and indeterminate campaign finance law. But when disclosure obligations attach to the exercise of First Amendment rights, an institutional speaker must often determine, even before it speaks, whether publishing will require registration, financial reporting, and the disclosure of the identities of its supporters. The question the case at hand raises is whether the First Amendment allows a state to impose those obligations on an organization that simply publishes discussions of public policy. Alaska Policy Forum, a nonprofit research organization, published materials criticizing ranked-choice voting just before Alaskans considered a ballot initiative to adopt it. APF’s publications never mentioned the initiative by name. The Alaska Public Offices Commission treated them as regulated electoral communications anyway, relying on their language and timing, and found that compensated employee time was the expenditure triggering Alaska’s registration, reporting, and disclosure requirements. The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed, and Cato has now filed an amicus brief supporting APF’s petition for certiorari. For more than 50 years, our nation’s Supreme Court has continued to narrow the means by which government may regulate political spending. Compelled disclosure itself burdens association, as NAACP v. Alabama (1958) held. And as McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission (1995) put it, the simple interest in providing voters with additional relevant information does not justify a requirement that a writer make statements or disclosures she would otherwise omit. Alaska’s regime cannot be reconciled with the Court’s jurisprudence. In Buckley v. Valeo (1976), a disclosure provision reached anyone who made expenditures for the purpose of influencing a federal election. The Court held that the ambiguity of that phrase posed constitutional problems, because that phrase could encompass both issue discussion and advocacy of a political result, and construed it to reach only communications expressly advocating the election or defeat of a clearly identified candidate. McConnell v. FEC (2003) later allowed a broader category, but only because BCRA’s definition supplied criteria that were both easily understood and objectively determinable. Alaska’s standard meets neither requirement. The State uses the label of express advocacy but defines that term by what an audience would take a communication to mean, a perspective the speaker cannot know in advance. It asks whether speech, read as a whole and with limited reference to outside events, is susceptible of no other reasonable interpretation than an exhortation to vote, and lets timing and the audience’s presumed knowledge of the ballot decide the result. The Court has twice rejected that method. Buckley declined to analyze the question in terms of intent and of effect, because that perspective would afford no security for free discussion. And in FEC v. Wisconsin Right to Life (2007), the Court rejected tests resting on the actual effect speech will have on an election or on a segment of the target audience, holding that where doubt remains, the tie goes to the speaker, not the censor. Alaska has combined three speech-chilling features: a contextual rule for classifying speech, an expenditure definition that includes ordinary employee time, and a threshold beginning at the first dollar. Together they require a policy organization to conduct its own campaign finance analysis before publishing its own research. Vagueness, as Buckley noted, is particularly treacherous where violation carries criminal penalties. Speakers facing an uncertain boundary steer far wider of the unlawful zone. Speech is chilled even if no penalty ever issues, because the risk of a chilling effect on association is enough. Cato’s brief argues that the Court should grant the petition and reaffirm that the presence of a public question on a ballot does not diminish the freedom to discuss any issue related to it. Director, Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, Cato Institute Every weekday morning: independent analysis grounded in individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and peace.

The day before David come home in 2021, myself, my husband, and my daughter, Tuesday, we were all called to the sheriff's office for a meeting with the DA and David at the time, Leatherwood, their authorities. The sheriff was there. Yeah, I believe it was in February. Briefly, Judge. Ms. Hunt, at the time all this happened, November 13th, 2017, did your home have running water? Had you not had running water in a period around then? No, ma'am. We had one area of the house that was sluggish because of the salt buildup that went into the back bathroom, but it was just in that bathroom and they got that fixed in the tub. We did have slow running water in the front. We had... My husband and David both had to replace the water lines. Time period, I can't tell you the exact time period, but there was running water. I had water in my kitchen, water in my bathroom. That's where the girls took their bath was in my bathroom. Ms. Hunt, you mentioned earlier with Mr. Britt that the dogs would sleep inside the house? And you said Bubbles, the small one, and Sapphire, a bigger dog were just in the living area? Yes. Bubbles was above Paitin's head on the arm of the couch. Sapphire was somewhere in there. She always is. I did not see Sapphire, but I was not looking for Sapphire. I was looking at Paitin. Well, just at any point during this trial, you may be recalled to come and testify again. So, that means that when they call to ask you to testify, then you have to adhere to your obligations of the subpoena. At this time, you may step down. I'm assuming you don't need it today, is it correct? (02:03:04)All right, sir, if you can please take the witness stand. You can go ahead and place your left hand on the Bible. Raise your right hand. The clerk will swear you in. Do you solemnly swear that the testimony you give in court today will be the truth, the whole truth, nothing but the truth, so help you God? Sir, as you testify here today, please make sure to speak loudly and clearly into that microphone so everybody here can hear you. Please make sure all of your answers are out loud. No head shakes or nods or mm-hmm. Everything has to be a yes or a no, and please wait for the attorney to be done asking their question before you give any sort of response. Can you do that? Can you state your name and spell it for the jury, please? And around the November 12th, 13th, 14th timeframe of 2017, where did you reside? And were you married to Lisa Hunt, who just testified? And you've been in the courtrooms while Ms. Hunt was testifying, correct? How long have you raised or been around Mr. Prevatte? I'm his father. There was a sperm donor. I'm his father. Yes, sir. Matter of fact, he's going to get his name changed to Hunt. Now, I'm going to take you to November 13th, 2017 or November 12th. Who was living in your house at the time? Okay. And how long had Savannah and Paitin lived with you prior to 2017? I want to talk about the house. You lived at 104 Blackwater Drive? If you walk in the door, there's a kitchen to the right, and there's another door up beside the fireplace, and it's on the left, and that's the master bedroom. Okay. And then Savannah and Paitin, did they have their own room? No. Mostly they slept on the couch, just like my daughter and my son, my neighbor was little, that's where they preferred to sleep was on the couch. Lisa said that David was inside the house sometimes and would live outside the house sometimes. When David was living inside the house, where would he sleep? Okay. When you say his bedroom, there were two other bedrooms other than yours and Lisa's room? Where would David sleep in relation to the front bedroom or back bedroom? The girls would have a bunch of their stuff in there too? All right. So, on November 12th, 13th, nobody else lived in the house but you, Lisa, Savannah, Paitin, and David, is that correct? And prior to that Sunday, November 12th, when did David come back home? He had left for some time and came back home when? At this time, November 12th and 13th, were you employed? Back then, I was loading hogs. I leave the house about 2:00, 3:00 in the afternoon. I wouldn't get home sometimes anywhere from 3:00 to 8:00 the next morning. Okay. On November 12th, at some point you had an injury, is that right? Yes, sir. I quit loading hogs and started working sow farm, and I had about a 400 pound sow take my knee and shift it over to the side, so I was out, messed up my ACL, and I was out of work for about three months. Okay. And on November 12th, were you still out of work or were you coming back into work? I started back. I was only for work for about a week before all this happened. What were your hours then when you came back to work after your injury? I used to be out there on the farm about 6:00 in the morning because you had to wash and shower again before you even got in there, so no contamination. So, I'd get to work about 5:30 and I'd go and take a shower and sit there and read my Bible until it was time to go to work. Usually about 4:00 unless we had hogs go out and then we had to clean the pens and then use about six or seven. All right. And would you work seven days a week or what days of the week did you work? I work two weeks straight and then have a weekend off. Okay. So, let's go back to, and I know it's hard, it's been a long time, but let's go back to November 12th. That's a Sunday evening. Did you work that Sunday? No, sir. I had that weekend off. We wound up going to my mother- in-law's. I had to put some safety rails up for her because she just had her knee surgery done and I was putting rails up for around a porch and a bathroom and a tub and everything so she can have something to grab on when she was moving. Okay. And who went out to Lumberton that weekend with you? That was me, my wife, my son and my two granddaughters. Yeah. I'm sorry. I started using their names. Yes, sir. Would you return to work or supposed to return to work that Monday then? So, when you would have to be out at the farm at 5:30 in the morning, I usually got up around about 4:00 in the morning so I could get up, get my coffee in me, and I would read my Bible something there too. Just get a good day started. And then I'd go to work. I would listen to my preaching on work and I sit out there and got dressed, took a shower, and then I'd go up there. I had what they call a daily book. If you've ever been to Christian, you know what I'm talking about? They got their prescription in there for different days. So, let me ask you then, if you had to get up at, I don't know, 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning- ... what time would you go to bed the previous night? About seven, seven, eight, give or take. All right. So, now I'm going to go to November 12th, that Sunday. Y'all were back from Lumberton. You know you have to go to work on the 13th, that Monday. About the same, but you know what I mean? Around 4:35. Okay. Then on the night of the 12th, who all was at the house at the night of the 12th? All right. And at some point, what time do you go to bed? Then when you go to bed, is David there or is he somewhere else or do you know? And when you say his friends, do you know their names? I know Jamie and Andrew. Oh, a guy named Michael, I think is what his name is, and a few other kids that I didn't know. I used to let them hang out in my house and have a bonfire. That way I know they were safe. All right. So you go to bed, David's outside, Savannah, Paitin and Lisa are inside when you go to bed? And that's normal, you normally sleep at night in your bedroom? Yes, sir. Usually I go in there and lay down. Usually the grand babies that come in there and lay with me. And I don't know something, I can put one of them to sleep. If they don't want me to go to sleep, they get in there with papa. I start rocking, singing a little bit and they say ... I know they're asleep. Lisa come and pick one up, take her to bed and bring the other one in and I knock her out. Lisa takes her to bed. All right. So you go to bed between 8:00 or 9:00 that night. Then at some point you wake up early morning hours of November 13th. All right. At some point, did Savannah ever come into your room? Yes, sir. I think I was falling back asleep and she came in there and told me that the baby was acting silly, that Paitin was acting silly, and I thought they were just in there playing. And I told her to go back to bed. I have no idea 'cause I wasn't looking at my clock or nothing else. It was dark. Well, let's stop. Just let me ask the questions and you answer the questions. So you tell her, she comes in there and says, "Something's wrong with Paitin." Yes, sir. "She's acting silly," I think, it was what she was saying, crazy or silly. I can't remember the exact words, sir. And you said, "Go on back in there and go to sleep." And at some point, do you go all the way back to sleep or do you- About time to get up and she goes in there to make my cup of coffee, make her coffee so I can get up and start going. I went in there and she was holding the baby and she said, "Baby, something ain't wrong. Ain't something right wrong. Ain't something wrong." Said, "Call 911." You know what I mean? I couldn't, but I trust my wife's instinct and I knew something was wrong. Sir, that's when I said, "Let's call 911." And then I went in there and started getting dressed. David came out, we got dressed and 911 didn't answer. So that's when we came up with the idea, let's jump in the car and get there. 'Cause by the time the ambulance gets to Pender County and come back, you know what I mean? I could already be at Pender County. Boo Boo. Who's that? I mean, that's his nickname. I'm sorry. I've been calling him since he was a kid. David. All right. And David has Paitin and where does he get into? All right. You've heard Lisa here testify it took about- You're saying it took you about four or five minutes? Yes, sir. You can ask Leatherwood because Leatherwood timed it. He asked me how did I get there so quick from a 911 call until they actually seen David there. And I asked him, "Could I go to jail if I tell them?" He told me no. And I said I averaged out about 120, topped out at 160. Were you able to see while you were driving what Paitin looked like at that Time? I kept my eye on the road going that fast, but I could smell when she defecated and that's when I really punched it. I couldn't tell you. Like I said, my eyes were on the road. You end up getting to Pender County Memorial to the ER? My son got out, banged on the door, and while he was banging on the door, I took my car 'cause I didn't want my car to be right there where the ambulance comes in at, and I took my car and I parked it around in the parking lot and I came through the front door. All right. At some point, was Paitin transferred to New Hanover County? All right. And did you travel down to New Hanover County? I went down 117 and then hit Castle Hayne Road that way and went 'cause it's the fastest way to go. Did anybody ride with you down to the New Hanover Hospital? She was in our van taking Savannah and everything down there. I don't know if she took my mom with her or not, 'cause my mom came out there at Pender County too. All right. And you at some point get down to New Hanover Hospital? Do you get to see Paitin at the hospital when she was in New Hanover? I got to see her when they was bringing her out the, what you call it, and act like they didn't want me to touch her or do nothing with her and I didn't know what was going on. I'm going, "Why not?" And that's when the security guard said, "You got to wait till a cop come here before you can even see her or anything 'cause they got to ask you some questions." And it was dragging on and dragging on. I told that security guard, "He's got five more minutes to get a cop here 'cause him and his buddy can't stop me from going in that room. I guarantee you won't [inaudible 02:19:15]." All right. So at some point, did Detective Leatherwood come and talk to you at the hospital? Okay. All right. And you talked to Detective Leatherwood while you were at the hospital? Let me take you back to the night of November 12th. You said previously that at the house that night, inside your house- ... I know of. Like I said, I was in bed and I don't think David was inside the house. I think he was outside with his friends. And where do they live? Do they live outside, inside? Or ... In and ... Both, in and out. I mean, they leave in in the night and we let them out the first thing in the morning when I go to work so they can use the restroom and everything. And Lisa's there in the daytime, so then I let them back in the house so they don't try to follow me down the road. All right. Did you see anybody inside your house the night of the 12th going into the early morning hours of the 13th? Okay. Did you see David come back into the house or hear David come back to the house as Lisa described? Outside of waking up around the time that Savannah comes into your room, did you wake up between the time you went to bed at 8:00 or 9:00 in the morning to the time that Savannah comes into your room? Did you wake up any other- Just to go take a pee. I used the restroom and then I was coming back laying down and that's when she came into the restroom and told me that. All right. So from the time 8:00 or nine o'clock on the 12th to the time you got up to the restroom- Did you go into the living room with the girls at all between the time you go to bed at 8:00 or 9:00 to the time you go to the restroom? No, sir. I usually go in there and check on them, but for some morning I didn't. I looked in the room, you know, I looked through the door 'cause of the what you call it right there, I seen Savannah standing up and I seen Paitin laying down. I thought she was asleep, so I went on and laid back down to bed. All right. So you didn't go in there into the living room with the girls between the time you went to bed, 8:00 or 9:00 that night to the time you woke up to go to the bathroom? No, sir. I just peeked then I'm on through the door while I was going back to the bathroom. And then as you're getting in the bed, Savannah comes in and says... I can't tell you. It might have been five, might have been 10, you know what I mean? But somewhere around there. All right. She comes in, you send her out, or you tell her to go back to bed? All right. At some point after Savannah tells you that something was funny with Paitin, does Lisa wake up? When it got about time for the alarm to come up, you know what I mean? She woke up right before the alarm come on to go make my coffee. Okay. And you heard that Lisa testified just now that she woke up when you went to go to the bathroom. Did you hear that? Yes. She usually now ... That's something if I get out of bed, she will pop her eyes out. I don't know what it is. She knows when her husband gets up out of that bed. At some point you're told by medical personnel or by Pender County Sheriff's Office what happened to Paitin, correct? Yeah. The guy from Pender County came in there and told me I had a very, very sick granddaughter, that they got her under ... Her seizures under control and that she's very sick and she's going to have to go to New Hanover. Yes, sir. Like I said, we had Savannah since she was 10 days old. I spoiled my grand babies. Yes, sir. Just briefly. Mr. Hunt, you and Savannah share the same birthday, don't you? You had an opportunity to see David with both of the girls, hadn't you? How would you describe his relationship with both of the girls? He loves his niece. He spoiled him just as much as I did. I just popped in my head. That was when he was little. He reminded me of a Boo Boo and that's just what it came ever since he was about 19-months-old, two-years-old. It's stuck, and everybody says when something happens, they say, "Well, it's the boo-boo. He's spoiled. He's the baby. It's the boo-boo." Which was it? She wake you up or did you wake up on your own? Like I said, I just went and used the bathroom. I was laying back down. I hadn't quite fallen asleep yet when she came in there. She said that, "Paitin was in there." I want to say, "She was acting silly." I thought they was just in there playing, so I told her to go back to sleep and let her sister go back to sleep, 'cause Savannah went to sleep a lot earlier than her sister did that night 'cause she got in trouble for walking Savannah around with a dog leash on her neck. To Paitin, yes, sir. She had a dog leash around her neck. And so when you told Savannah to go back into the living room and go back to sleep, did she do what you told her? Did she go back in there? Yes, sir. My wife takes care of us. If I got to work, she makes sure I'm taken care of. And so you knew she got up and walked out of the bedroom? She was holding Savannah and saying, "Something ain't right, baby. Something ain't right. She's having a seizure." Now, were you aware that Savannah had been sick the day before? Yes, sir. Matter of fact, I think Friday, my wife took her to a doctor's or something or some emergency room or something, but she had a doctor appointment the next day, that Monday. And who would normally take her to the doctor? Lisa? And so when you heard Lisa scream, you just jumped out of bed? Yeah, 'cause it was the most banshee-ist ... I knew something was wrong from that scream. So you had not gotten up and started to get dressed, you jumped out of bed? And then when you came into the living room, was David already there? And the clothes that we saw him wearing in the video at the hospital? And so, did you stay in the room or did you go back to the bedroom? I went back to the bedroom and got changed, put some clothes on so we can go to the emergency room. Where was Paitin when you went back to the bedroom? I don't know. I can't tell you if Lisa was holding her or by then Boo Boo was holding her. So there came a point when you came out and you were dressed, y'all made a decision to go- Yes, sir. When that emergency call didn't come in, we weren't going to wait another ... 'Cause we didn't know how long it would be. When he got into the car, did he continue to hold her? I remember him, like, at one time I told him I kept my eye on the road, but I remember looking over here and giving him mouth-to-mouth. He was giving her mouth-to-mouth 'cause that's when she defecated and he said, "Daddy, let's go." And that's when I hit 160. So you were aware that she had lost control of her bowel? When you got to the hospital, were David's clothes wet or dry? They was wet to where she lost control of her body fluids. And so you dropped David ... You pulled into the ambulance bay, David gets out and he bangs on the door? Yes, sir. And I take my car and I drive around to the parking lot and I come through the front door. So David is the one who rushes her into the emergency room? No, sir. She was back in one of those rooms in the back. I think he was in the room back there. When I got back there, I think he was in the room and I was in the room and they kicked us both out the room saying, "You know what I mean? There ain't enough room to get to work on her." And so did you stay in the lobby or did you go outside? What'd you do? I think I stayed in the lobby for a minute and then I went outside and smoked me a cigarette, waited for Lisa to get there, and I think we came, me and Lisa and them came back in together. Did you ask David if he knew what was going on with her? No, sir. I don't think so. Oh, we had a doctor come ... After Lisa came in there, we had a doctor come out there and that's when he told us that we had a very sick girl, but they got the seizures under control, but she was going to have to go to New Hanover. Greater care, which I didn't think it must have been that bad since it took two and a half hours for the ambulance to get there, 'cause when I went to take Boo Boo home so he could change his clothes, they were sitting right there at Shell's getting them some food and a cup of coffee. And when I come back, they were still sitting at Shell's. And so you took David home, he changed his clothes. Did y'all leave to go back to the hospital together? Yes or no, was there any conversation between you and David while you were going back to the hospital? And at some point, did anyone at New Hanover come out and speak to you, Lisa, and David about Paitin's condition? They wouldn't let us have nothing to do with her in New Hanover. We couldn't go nowhere around her. Only as far as we could get was in the parking lot. Yes, sir. He put us in the interview room, and that's when I told him, I said, "When she wakes up, she can tell you what in the world is going on." I think she was in there. I think she's the first one they took back there. Yeah. We were all emotions. I was in the parking lot begging God to take my life. I've been here 50-some years. The stuff I've done, I don't deserve to live, you know. And so when you returned home from New Hanover, was David at the house? Eventually, did David leave with Jamie or did he remain there at home? And to your knowledge, did he spend the night there that night or did he go to- Did David spend the night, Monday, at home with you and Lisa, or did he go somewhere else? Okay. All right. Thank you. I don't have any other questions at this time. Redirect, just briefly. You just said that you've done stuff you've done, you don't deserve to live. What'd you do? Yeah, I was mean when I was young. I used to fight all the time. All right, sir, you're still subject to the obligation of your subpoena, so that means if they call you again to testify, you have to come back and testify. Move this chair. Please come this way. Watch your step, sir. Mm-hmm. [inaudible 02:36:12] exit the [inaudible 02:36:13]. All right. Counsel can approach. All right, members of the jury, there's a bit of a sickness going around. So what we're going to do is we're going to break for the day, allow you an extra little bit of time for the weekend. So go ahead and close up your notebooks. Go ahead and take off your red badges, pin them to your notebooks. Now, as you go home for the weekend, remind you again, do not discuss this case amongst yourselves and do not discuss this case with anybody else. There may be more people that you interact with this weekend than you interacted with during this week. Those people are also going to be curious, and you are also going to have to explain to them that you are forbidden from speaking with them about this case. You are also forbidden from having any contact with any of the parties, attorneys, or witnesses. (02:38:02)You cannot conduct any independent investigation or inquiry. If you happen to go by any of the locations that were mentioned, you may pass by them, but you are not allowed to stop. Obviously, if there are any emergencies that require you to go to the hospital, you may do so, but not to conduct any independent investigation. You're not to post online on any social media sites regarding your experience as a juror or any of the evidence you've seen or heard. You're also not allowed to have anybody discuss this case in your presence. So you are excused. We will reconvene again Monday morning at 9:30. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honor. Make sure your notebooks are closed once again and your juror badge is attached the same way as those in your chairs and ready front row, then back this way, please. Quiet in the courtroom, please. Ma'am, quiet in the courtroom. Thank you, sir. Let the record reflect that the jury has exited the courtroom. We had, there were a number of bench conferences. First was Mr. Britt's concern regarding our poor clerk. He definitely was not feeling very well. We had another one just before the jury broke that I indicated that we were just going to break for the remainder of the day, given the sickness that might be going around. The bailiff with the jurors came up and approached me. He said a juror had asked him about asking the bailiff questions regarding the trial. I'm going to have him come back in and explain that on the record just so that we all know exactly what was asked. As far as this session is concerned, it is the Friday after the Monday in which this trial calendar had begun. (02:40:25)The session not having concluded during the pendency of this week. Court retains jurisdiction regarding this case and any other matters on the trial calendar, and we will continue the matter through next week or until its conclusion. And I'll enter an order extending the session. Is there anything that we need to discuss on behalf of the state while we're waiting for the bailiff to come back in? All right. If you want to just let him know that as soon as he's ready to come back in the courtroom. Thank you. (02:41:28)Mr. Bailiff, you indicated that a juror had asked you a question. Can you explain that question again? Yes. Juror number eight was asking in reference to the proceedings outside of the courtroom setting, would he be able to ask me any questions? And then I immediately informed you of same, Your Honor. All right. Thank you. Anything you wish to say regarding that, Mr. Britt? All right. Then we will go ahead and be in recess until Monday morning at 9:30. If the parties here can remain and if we can go off audio and the video. Anybody- Luckily for you, we deliver. title: NFL today: How to watch Chiefs v Raiders, TV channels & live stream Sunday 4 October - The Guardian
content: How will the Chiefs and Raiders fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options Disorienting as it may sound given the past 12 years of Chiefs-Raiders matchups, their game Sunday in Las Vegas is one of the blockbusters of the young NFL season. Kansas City have used Las Vegas (and before that, Oakland) as a doormat since the 2015 season, when Patrick Mahomes was a sophomore at Texas Tech. The Chiefs took both games from the Raiders that year and began a run of 18 wins in the teams’ last 22 contests, an unusual run of AFC West dominance in a league that adores parity. The Chiefs are favored again this week, but by less than a touchdown. The Silver and Black come in sporting a matching 3-0 record with their Missourian visitors. Kirk Cousins has found the fountain of youth at 38, keeping No 1 draft pick Fernando Mendoza in an understudy’s role for at least a while longer. The 38-year-old has averaged at least 7.5 yards per pass attempt in each of the team’s three wins, two of which came on the road. The Raiders have benefited from a light opening schedule, taking advantage of games against the moribund Dolphins and Saints. Now comes a stiff test in the desert. United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Football, or stream with NOW. Just how back is Patrick Mahomes? The answer might be “extremely.” The franchise QB was having the worst season of his career last year even before it ended a few weeks early because of a torn ACL. But now, Mahomes looks both accurate and unusually spry, like a man who’s gained mobility from chasing a bunch of little kids around his house. He is also benefiting massively from the arrival of Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker at running back. Walker is the league’s leading rusher, with 360 yards in his first three games with K.C. It’s not just volume, either; his 5.8 yards per touch are a career best. Cousins is getting the publicity, but the Raiders’ greatest strength to date is one that should come in extra handy against Mahomes: their sublime pass rush. Only one club, the Vikings, have generated more pressures than Vegas, according to Pro Football Reference. The biggest chunk of those (13) have come from the freakishly good Maxx Crosby, who only remains with the team because the Ravens backed out of a trade the teams had agreed to in March. It’s a team effort, though: Crosby only has two of the Raiders’ 10 sacks to date, a figure that places them tied for fourth. Mahomes will be minding his blind side.

title: Poetry Moment: 'to be the bird' by nicole v basta - WPSU
content: This is Poetry Moment on WPSU – a weekly program featuring the work of contemporary Pennsylvania poets. Your host is poet and author Marjorie Maddox, a 2023 Monson Arts Fellow, author of more than 20 books, and Professor Emerita of English and Creative Writing at the Lock Haven campus of Commonwealth University. Welcome to Poetry Moment. I’m Marjorie MaddoxWho hasn't, at some point, yearned to be a bird? In today's poem, "to be the bird," nicole v basta considers the storks of Poland, where, before moving to Pennsylvania, her ancestors lived, eventually working in the coal mines and garment factories of Wilkes-Barre. nicole v basta (who does not use capital letters in her name) is a 2026 Academy of American Poets Laureate Fellow. Her poems have appeared in Ploughshares, Blackbird, Third Coast, North American Review, and elsewhere. Her second chapbook, "the next field over" (2022), was published by Tolsun Books. nicole is also a community educator, arts events producer, and visual artist. Her work has been supported by grants and residencies, including Art Farm Nebraska, Monson Arts, and The Saltonstall Foundation. Currently, she is Poet Laureate of Tompkins County/Ithaca, New York. I'm told that, in Poland, storks migrate large distances to winter in Africa. After that long absence, their return is met with great anticipation. According to one source, "the sight of a stork circling overhead or tending to its massive nest is more than just a glimpse of nature; it’s a symbol of rebirth, good fortune, and deep cultural connection."... [S]torks restoring their nests. . . is a potent symbol [both] of renewal" and warmer days ("Storks: Poland's Beloved Harbingers of Spring"). In her poem, "to be the bird," nicole v basta also welcomes this majestic bird, embracing its "kind of solitude" as a gift. on the roof, a stork nests and dreams of a past lifewading in the shallow water of another continent beneath the roof, a woman goes on with her luckkneels to the narrow altar in the home she made of her body alone— suppose the silence after a quest-ion begins a new day, the quiet bouncing off the brims of hats— words like spar and spark, shoulder, the secondstar, limp in the air like lazy ghosts and suppose the answers arrive as the birds, not as the birthsthey've come to represent in the west, no, we're in the old country now and it is a gift, that kind of solitudethe one when there is no echo of yourself who breathes and what i am saying is— i may only wantto be the bird Originally published in Colorado Review Volume 50, Number 1, Spring 2023 Listen for Poetry Moment with Marjorie Maddox, Mondays during Morning Edition and All Things Considered on WPSU. You'll find more episodes at https://radio.wpsu.org/show/poetry-moment Have a tip for the WPSU newsroom? Email radionews@psu.edu.
